scope: Eight exact current research releases with readable scheme evidence and explicit bit-RAM recovery baselines. Local research draft; no scientific admission or changes to challenge parameters.
label_policy: A labels identify stated premises only. The preview assigns stable global labels and retains them across note revisions; retiring a premise leaves a numbering gap rather than reusing its label. Display relevant premises in numeric label order. Stable premise IDs and exact profile_ids carry identity. Scheme-security gaps are separate tasks, carry no A label and are not attack prerequisites.

teaching-dh-kem@7.title: Finite-field DH: agreement and the recovery problem
teaching-dh-kem@7.summary: Fifty certified groups pair a simple agreement identity with a limited classical attack reference. This custom research KEM has an explicit short-exponent distribution.

sections.title: From shared-element hardness to key secrecy
sections.body:
For this stage, \(X=g^x\), \(C=g^r\), and \(Z=g^{xr}\), with independent uniform \(x,r\in\{1,\ldots,M\}\). This exact short-exponent distribution matters.

For a classical adversary making at most \(Q\) hash queries, the argument in Full text gives
\[
 \Pr[\text{recover the complete key}]\le 2^{-256}+Q\varepsilon_j+\delta_j.
\]
Here \(\varepsilon_j\) bounds recovery of \(Z\) at the reduction's stated budget, and \(\delta_j\) is the concrete-hash transfer allowance. Key-versus-random distinguishing advantage is at most \(Q\varepsilon_j+\delta_j\). Bounds are capped at one.

These are conditional, quantitative relationships—not assigned security bits. Small stages can have large \(\varepsilon_j\). The experiment has one fresh honest challenge and no decapsulation or key-checking oracle; it makes no IND-CCA claim.

sections.title: What this secrecy argument covers
sections.body: The scoped passive argument is developed in Security and Full text. It covers the exact short-exponent distribution and transcript input, under explicit computational and hash-transfer premises. It does not establish IND-CCA, multi-session composition, constant-time execution or a numerical security level.

sections.title: Every honest pair agrees
sections.body:
The certified parameters give a prime-order subgroup, and \(1\le x,r\le M<q\). Its nonzero exponents ensure valid nonidentity public values and shared element. For every such pair,
\[
 (g^x)^r=(g^r)^x\pmod p.
\]
Encapsulation and decapsulation encode the same profile, parameters, public key, ciphertext and shared element, so their SHA-256 inputs are identical. Honest disagreement is exactly zero in this mathematical experiment. No hardness or random-oracle premise is needed; deterministic hashing is enough. Full text checks the certificate, range and encoding steps. This is not a proof of fault-free execution or side-channel resistance.

sections.title: Reading the classical curve
sections.body:
The frozen reference compares subgroup rho, interval search, and a normalized number-field-sieve shape. With field bit length \(L\) and \(F(L)=(L\ln2)^{1/3}[\ln(L\ln2)]^{2/3}\), its ingredients are
\[
\tfrac12\log_2q,\qquad128F(L)/F(3072),\qquad\tfrac12\log_2M.
\]
The adapter freezes and rounds its baseline before choosing \(M\); its recorded minimum is authoritative. Normalizing to 128 at 3072 bits is a project convention. These are heuristic work exponents, not gate counts, seconds or a lower bound on all attacks. Reused groups can permit preparation to be shared across targets.

The formula is a frozen asymptotic reference, not a complete finite-parameter attack specification with a success-normalized cost. Its heuristic dependencies have not been individually formalized in this note; an empty labelled-premise list does not make the estimate unconditional.

sections.title: Scope of the classical attack comparison
sections.body:
The curve combines declared rho, interval and NFS approximations for these exact groups and exponent intervals. Constants, memory and amortized preparation need separate accounting. The roughly sixteen reference bits reserved for interval search are a design margin inside this model, not a proved security margin.

An omitted or faster attack changes the best available attack comparison; it does not by itself invalidate the stated algorithm's own cost. The present material does not isolate a sufficiently precise additional premise to label here. A new attack result should state its algorithm, success, units, preprocessing scope and any actual dependencies, retaining its own version rather than silently rewriting the historical curve.

sections.title: A quantum route without a resource curve
sections.body: Shor's algorithm gives a polynomial-time route to finite-field discrete logarithms on a sufficiently capable quantum computer. No configuration-specific gate, qubit, error-correction or elapsed-time budget is published here. A blank quantum graph means unquantified work, not zero cost or half the classical exponent.

sections.title: Interval computational Diffie–Hellman
sections.body:
Fix primes \(p,q\) with \(q\mid p-1\), an element \(g\in\mathbb F_p^*\) of order \(q\), and an integer \(1\le M<q\). Sample \(x,y\) independently and uniformly from \(\{1,\ldots,M\}\). Given \((p,q,g,M,g^x,g^y)\), the task is to output \(g^{xy}\). The interval-CDH premise at budget \(T\) is: every classical algorithm \(A\) using at most \(T\) bit operations, including preparation, satisfies \(\Pr[A(p,q,g,M,g^x,g^y)=g^{xy}]\le\varepsilon\). All group elements are canonically encoded; field arithmetic is available to the attacker.

### Use in this construction

For each release-7 profile \(j\), fix its certified \((p_j,q_j,g_j)\) and set \(M_j=\min\{q_j-1,2^{\lceil2b_j+32\rceil}-1\}\), where \(b_j\) is the immutable six-decimal reference value used by `exponent_upper_bound`. The key and encapsulation exponents are independent uniform integers from \(1\) through \(M_j\). Instantiate \(T=T'\) and \(\varepsilon=\varepsilon_j\) in the Full text reduction; \(T'\) includes oracle simulation and extraction. The frozen reference defines this sampler, not a security theorem. Public group parameters remain fixed across instances.

### Scope and qualifications

Here \(T\) counts complete classical bit-RAM work, including preparation charged to this target; no uncharged secret advice or precomputed table is supplied. The probability includes the sampled inputs and the algorithm's coins. The claim is a finite-resource bound for the stated parameters, not an assertion that every small parameter choice is secure. A numerical guarantee requires an explicit \(T\) and \(\varepsilon\); none is established merely by writing the premise.

This is interval-CDH, not ordinary full-range CDH and not a discrete-logarithm premise. Computing either logarithm solves the task, but hardness of discrete logarithms alone does not establish hardness of CDH. [Shoup, section 14.1](https://www.shoup.net/papers/iso-2_1.pdf) defines ordinary CDH; the interval distribution here is an explicit variation taken from the exact sampler. The Full text proof retains its \(Q\)-query extraction loss and its separate concrete-hash premise. Honest correctness follows from group algebra and the checked parameter certificates; it needs neither hardness nor a random-oracle premise.

sections.title: Random-oracle transfer for transcript hashing
sections.body:
Fix a joint distribution \(D\) of a public transcript \(\tau\) and a hidden value \(Z\), and a public encoding \(F(\tau,Z)\) injective in \(Z\). Let \(K=h(F(\tau,Z))\in\{0,1\}^{256}\). Write \(R_h\) for the best probability of recovering all of \(K\) from \(\tau\), and \(I_h\) for the best absolute difference between output-1 probabilities given \((\tau,K)\) or \((\tau,U_{256})\). Both range over classical attackers with the same stated work and hash-query budgets, without a decryption oracle. Define \(R_H,I_H\) by replacing the transcript hash with a shared random oracle \(H\). The transfer premise is \(R_h\le R_H+\delta\) and \(I_h\le I_H+\delta\).

### Use in this construction

Here \(h=\mathrm{SHA256}\). Draw the interval-DH transcript \(\tau=(j,p,q,g,X,C)\) with \(X=g^x\), \(C=g^y\), \(Z=g^{xy}\) and the exact independent interval sampler above. The domain is `crucible/teaching-dh-kem/v7/shared-secret` followed by a zero byte. Frame, in order, the profile ASCII and \(p,q,g,X,C,Z\); each integer uses \(\lceil\operatorname{bitlen}(p)/8\rceil\) big-endian bytes and each field has a four-byte big-endian length prefix. This defines \(D_j,F_j\); substitute \(\delta=\delta_j\). The Full text bound remains \(\min\{1,2^{-256}+Q\varepsilon_j+\delta_j\}\) for recovery and \(\min\{1,Q\varepsilon_j+\delta_j\}\) for distinguishing.

### Scope and qualifications

The work budget includes preparation charged to one target. Every classical hash query, including pre-challenge queries, counts toward \(Q\), and its length is bounded by \(B\); the resource convention is the one fixed in Full text. In the ideal experiment the challenger and attacker use the same random function; fixed public parameters and release-identification hashes are not randomized. There is no decapsulation/equality oracle, leakage, quantum query or multi-target claim.

This is an experiment-specific modeling premise. No numerical \(\delta\) has been proved or measured; setting it to zero is an idealization. It is not a claim that a known fixed function is indistinguishable from a random oracle by direct comparison, nor a consequence of collision resistance. [Canetti, Goldreich and Halevi](https://arxiv.org/abs/cs/0010019) show why a random-oracle proof does not generally justify a concrete instantiation. The present note's ideal-hash reduction is an adaptation, not an imported concrete-SHA-256 theorem. The honest-correctness proof requires only deterministic hashing and does not use this premise.

sections.title: One common measure of attack work
sections.body:
These curves use **Classical bit-RAM v1**: elementary Boolean operations and one-bit memory transfers share a fixed accounting rule. All attack setup is charged to one fresh challenge. Memory capacity is unlimited in this abstraction, and the storage bound remains visible beside the graph.

The plotted quantity is \(\log_2 W\), where \(W\) bounds a specified strategy's work and its stated assumptions imply at least **50% probability of recovering the complete shared key**. These are reproducible **baseline upper bounds**, not the cheapest known attacks or a security lower bound. A bigger value does not establish a more secure scheme. Full text contains the cost rules, proofs, parameter table and reproduction commands.

sections.title: Interval baby-step–giant-step
sections.body:
Baby-step–giant-step searches the actual published exponent interval. It recovers the recipient exponent, computes the shared group element, and applies the scheme's exact transcript hash. The displayed work is a conservative upper bound with success one for honest inputs. No random-walk assumption is needed. The large table is explicitly included. This is a reproducible baseline, not the cheapest known finite-field attack; number-field-sieve and reusable-precomputation improvements are absent.

For an exponent interval \(1\le x\le M\), the table has \(m=\lceil\sqrt{M+1}\rceil\) entries. The work includes building and sorting it, every lookup and the final shared-key derivation.

teaching-dh-kem@7.full_text_appendix:
## Reproducible bit-RAM attack analysis

## Shared computation model: crucible-bit-ram-v1

The program is uniform in public configuration inputs; no answer-dependent
advice is permitted. Its fixed-address bit registers support arbitrary Boolean
functions of one or two bits at unit cost. Constants, fixed wiring and fixed bit
permutations are free. A dynamically addressed bit read or write costs one;
computing that address is additional charged arithmetic. This is a bit-RAM
abstraction inspired by NIST's classical gate-count discussions, not the CAT
pure circuit metric and not a NIST-approved scheme classification.

The baseline has no memory-cap constraint. It measures neither physical latency
nor energy. A pointer of b bits must be manipulated with the b-bit arithmetic
account. Loops use a public counter width and charge increment/comparison.
Input generation for the honest challenger is outside the attack budget; all
attacker initialization, candidate generation, verification and key derivation
are inside. Randomness and any rejection sampling need explicit budgets or
their own success-loss treatment. A counter on high-level Python operations is
validation of the operation census, not a trace of exact elementary gates.

Primitive upper bounds, for width w: ADD/SUB/CMP=8w; MUX=3w;
MODADD=24(w+1); MUL=16(w+1)^2; DIVMOD=64(w+1)^2;
MODMUL=80(w+1)^2; LOOP(b)=16(b+1).
MODPOW(w,e)=e(2 MODMUL(w)+MUX(w)+LOOP(e))+2w.
All bounds refer to schoolbook/ripple, restoring-division and double-and-add
algorithms. They deliberately upper-bound a particular implementation.

SHA-256/SHA-512 follow FIPS180-4. The schedule uses two small sigmas and three
word additions per expanded word. Each round uses two large sigmas, Ch, Maj,
and seven additions. Eight final additions update the chaining value. Padding
and block input/output are charged. SHA3/SHAKE follow FIPS202: Keccak-f[1600]
uses at most193536 Boolean operations (24 rounds of8064), padded to200000
for control. Absorption and output transfers are additional. These are
algorithmic upper bounds, not claims about optimized hardware.

Every profile's complete attack is stopped within its reported budget. Its
success statement names the probability space and any unproved premises.
The resulting curve is a documented attack upper bound, not a proven security
level and not necessarily the cheapest known attack. No 50%-success result is
inferred simply by dividing cost by average success probability.

Primary specifications:
- https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/FIPS/NIST.FIPS.180-4.pdf
- https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/FIPS/NIST.FIPS.202.pdf


## Reproduction

From this source checkout:
```text
python scripts/build_ram_attack_notes.py --check
python -m pytest tests/test_ram_common.py tests/test_ram_classical_attacks.py tests/test_ram_lattice_attacks.py tests/test_ram_code_attacks.py tests/test_ram_catalogue.py
```
The generated `crucible/data/ram_attack_curves.json` retains integer cost components, parameters, assumptions and source-file hashes. No cryptographic-size attack is executed. Small examples check implementation paths; they do not verify heuristic premises at large sizes. No external model service or paid API is used.

## Interval baby-step–giant-step

Worked configuration: dh-v7-tier-50. The same algorithm and parameterized formulas generate the other rows below.

Write every candidate x in [0,M] uniquely as x=im+j, with m=ceil(sqrt(M+1)), 0<=j<m and 0<=i<ceil((M+1)/m). Store (g^j,j), or (jG,j) for a curve, in a bottom-up mergesorted table. A giant-step lookup compares the target times g^(-im), or target-imG, against the table. Equality yields x; check x<=M and verify the public key. No probabilistic collision model or constant-time hash-table premise is used. The table has distinct group elements because m<=q. Binary search uses at most ceil(log2(m))+1 comparisons. Sorting uses at most m*ceil(log2(m)) comparisons and twice that many record transfers. Each comparison reads both full records and pays a bitwise comparison plus address/control work. Two table arrays are reserved in the memory bound. Records occupy padded power-of-two bit slots. Each bit address concatenates the record index with a fixed, unrolled offset; this avoids treating a variable address multiplication or an entire RAM word transfer as free. All padding is included in the storage bound. Eight counter-update/compare allowances per table control step cover the input/output pointers and branches. Here M=497323236409786642155382248146820840100456150797347717440463976893159497012533375533055, m=22300745198530623141535718272648361505980416, giant iterations=22300745198530623141535718272648361505980416, key width=3072, record width=3216 bits. All quantities are exact integers until the final log2 display. The work bound covers success probability one, hence also the shared 50% target. This does not assert the budget is minimal for achieving that target.

For this release the public certificates prove prime p,q and ord(g)=q; the honest x,r lie in [1,M] with M<q. Thus there is a unique x in that interval. The recovered x gives c^x=g^(rx). The final SHA-256 input has 2387 bytes including all uint32 framing, profile, p,q,g, X,C,Z. No hash collision-resistance hypothesis is needed to compute the same hash. The profile-specific public constants are part of the input specification; all baby-table preparation is charged again for each target.

Success statement for this worked configuration: 1

teaching-dh-kem@7.full_text_argument_appendix:
## Exact-release security and correctness argument

### Exact experiment and meaning of the claim

Fix one registered profile j, the published construction and all exact parameter bytes. Key generation emits a fresh honest public key; encapsulation emits one ciphertext C and a 256-bit key K. The public transcript includes the profile and parameters. The recovery adversary receives this transcript, not K, and outputs one 256-bit candidate; success means equality with **the entire key**, never recovery of half its bits. A participant's multiple guesses or multiple target instances require a separately counted game. The one-challenge distinguishing adversary additionally receives either K or an independent uniform 256-bit string. Its advantage is the absolute difference of its probability of outputting 1 in those two experiments, with no factor-of-two convention hidden in the definition. Neither adversary receives a decapsulation oracle, a correctness/equality oracle, private state or timing leakage. Public encapsulation can be performed by the adversary itself within its budget.

The theorem below concerns classical algorithms and classical oracle queries. T counts the complete attack work, including preparation charged to this target; Q bounds all hash queries, including those made before the challenge is supplied; B bounds their bit length. Public fixed parameters may be known before the challenge, but uncharged secret advice or a precomputed discrete-log table is not granted. Multi-target amortization is a different resource statement. These are finite-parameter success relations, not an asymptotic assertion that all 50 small and large stages are secure.

Write F(T_pub,Z) for the adapter's exact domain-separated, length-framed KDF input. In the ideal experiment the transcript KDF uses a uniformly random function H from bitstrings to 256-bit strings, shared consistently between challenger and adversary. Fixed release-identification hashes and public parameters remain public inputs; they are not re-randomized artifact identities. The public prefix is fixed by T_pub and the final encoded secret is injective. Let Hit mean that the adversary asks H at F(T_pub,Z).

### Why the exact-query event controls success

Lazy-sample H: keep a table, give a new independent uniform answer to each new input, and reuse it on repeats. If Hit never occurs, the value H(F(T_pub,Z)) has never been shown. Even conditioned on the whole non-Hit transcript and the adversary's output, that value remains uniform and independent. Therefore complete-key recovery has probability at most Pr[Hit] + 2^(-256). Collisions with another oracle output do not need a separate birthday term: an unseen target output is still uniform, and accidental equality is included in 2^(-256).

For distinguishing, compare the real-key game with a game that gives an independent uniform test key. Couple their coins and all oracle replies until the first target-input query. Before that query their distributions agree, including pre-challenge queries; if a target-input query already occurred, mark Hit before revealing the test key. Thus the difference of output-1 probabilities is at most Pr[Hit] in the independent-test-key game. That game is simulatable without knowing Z. The reductions below bound its Hit probability as well as recovery's Hit probability.

The lazy-oracle simulator can use a simple list, so its bookkeeping is at most O(Q^2(B+256)) bit operations and O(Q(B+256)) bits of memory, plus the explicitly stated extraction arithmetic and the adversary's work. This deliberately loose bound makes the reduction executable without treating hash-table lookup as a free operation. It is not a plotted concrete attack-cost estimate. An implementation with better lookup can tighten it; no numeric security level is inferred from the O notation.

### Concrete hash transfer and what has actually been proved

The random-oracle theorem is a mathematical statement in that model. For the implemented SHA-256 KDF, a separate premise specifies an additive transfer slack delta: for the declared adversary/resource class, real complete-key recovery is no more than the ideal recovery plus delta, and real distinguishing advantage is no more than ideal advantage plus delta. This premise applies to the exact framed-input construction, not to every use of SHA-256. It does not assert that a fixed public hash is indistinguishable from a random oracle under a naive direct comparison; such an assertion would be false. No bound on delta has been proved or measured here. Setting delta=0 is the usual ideal-model extrapolation, explicitly an assumption. Collision resistance alone does not supply this premise.

The reductions and algebra below are locally authored derivations. The cited literature supplies their lineage and relevant standard constructions, not an independent approval of this implementation. We have not proved source-code refinement, constant-time behavior, resistance to malformed inputs, multi-session security or IND-CCA. No one-hour limit or current attack plot is turned into a lower bound by these arguments.

### Distribution and injective transcript for release 7

The immutable profile supplies p,q,g. The exact bound M is returned by exponent_upper_bound: min(q-1,2^ceil(2b+32)-1), where b is that profile's frozen six-decimal reference. This defines the distribution; it is not used as hardness evidence. Sample x and r independently and uniformly in 1..M. Public setup is deterministic and reusable. KDF fields are profile ASCII, p,q,g, X,C,Z; every integer uses w=ceil(bit_length(p)/8) big-endian bytes, and each field is preceded by its four-byte big-endian length. The fixed domain is `crucible/teaching-dh-kem/v7/shared-secret\0`. Length prefixes and fixed field order make parsing unique; for a fixed public prefix, different Z values have different inputs. Only the exact query can reveal the ideal key.

### Extraction from a DH query

Given only a challenge (X,C) from the exact DH distribution, a solver runs the recovery adversary with a lazily sampled oracle. If a pre-challenge phase is allowed, it exposes X first and withholds C until that phase ends; the hidden honest challenge values can equivalently be sampled at the outset. All phase queries count toward Q. For a distinguishing adversary it also supplies an independent uniform test key. It records the at most Q oracle queries and chooses one of Q positions uniformly (unused positions produce failure). It accepts that query as a candidate only when its framing, profile, parameter bytes, X and C equal the target transcript and its final field is a valid canonical shared-element encoding; it returns that decoded element. If Hit occurred, at least one position contains the true Z, so this solver succeeds with probability at least Pr[Hit]/Q. It need not recognize which candidate is right and is given no DDH oracle. Only the selected candidate needs decoding: add O(B+L^3) bit operations with schoolbook modular arithmetic, where L is the field bit length. This covers the finite-field membership exponentiation or the prime-field compressed-point square root; these costs are included in T'.

Let S_j(T') be the maximum success of a solver for that exact computational-DH distribution within the simulation/extraction resource budget T'. The preceding construction proves Pr[Hit] <= Q*S_j(T'). Consequently
\[
 P_{\mathrm{recover}}^{\mathrm{RO}}(T,Q)\le \min\{1,2^{-256}+Q S_j(T')\},\qquad
 \operatorname{Adv}_{\mathrm{key}}^{\mathrm{RO}}(T,Q)\le\min\{1,Q S_j(T')\}.
\]
For Q=0 the respective bounds are 2^(-256) and zero. If a stated computational premise gives S_j(T') <= epsilon_j and the concrete-transfer premise gives delta_j, add delta_j to the corresponding right side and cap at one. This is a Q-loss reduction; it is not a tight concrete-security estimate. The premise needs an explicit epsilon_j and budget to assert a numerical guarantee. When a stage is easy, S_j may be close to one and the bound correctly becomes vacuous. Computing a discrete logarithm is a sufficient CDH solution; the theorem does not assume that it is the only route.

### Complete honest-correctness argument

For every embedded certificate, recurse to trial-divided primes below 2^16. An internal candidate n=2Rq+1 has certified prime q with q^2>n, 2^(n-1)=1 mod n, and gcd(2^(2R)-1,n)=1. For every prime divisor ell of n, the order of 2 modulo ell divides 2Rq but not 2R, hence is divisible by q; thus ell is at least q+1>sqrt(n). A composite n has a prime divisor at most sqrt(n), contradiction. This proves each n prime, then p and q. It is a direct instance of Pocklington's criterion; no probable-prime error remains.

The validator checks 1<g<p-1 and g^q=1. As q is prime, g has order q. For 1<=x,r<=M<=q-1, g^x and g^r are nonidentity subgroup elements. Since q is odd, -1 has order 2 and is not in this subgroup; therefore neither honest public value is the rejected p-1. Also xr is nonzero mod q, so Z is nonidentity. Thus honest encodings pass the decoder. Multiplication of integers is commutative, so exponent laws give (g^x)^r=g^(xr)=(g^r)^x. Decapsulation reconstructs precisely the public key g^x and preserves the received ciphertext. All seven framed KDF fields coincide byte for byte. Determinism of SHA-256 implies equal output; collision resistance and pseudorandomness are irrelevant to equality. This argument holds for every allowed pair, independent of how random choices happened, after successful setup validation.

Certificates establish prime/group facts, not interval-CDH hardness. The implementation uses variable-time Python arithmetic. The theorem is about specified mathematical operations and encodings; code refinement, fault behavior and leakage remain outside it. Existing conformance tests plus the deterministic boundary-pair check corroborate the implementation but do not replace this all-pairs proof.

statements.label: A-13

Write \(R_h\) for the best probability of recovering all of \(K\) from \(\tau\), and \(I_h\) for the best absolute difference between output-1 probabilities given \((\tau,K)\) or \((\tau,U_{256})\). statements.label: Security claim
statements.title: Passive key recovery and distinguishing
statements.definition:
For every registered native configuration of exact research release `teaching-dh-kem@7`, generate one fresh honest public key and one encapsulation. Let R be the supremum probability, among classical adversaries using at most T total computation work and the stated query budgets, of returning the complete 256-bit shared key in one output. Probability includes honest generation, encapsulation and the adversary's coins; condition on valid successful generation. Pre-challenge computation and designated hash queries count toward the same budgets.

Let \(Q\) bound transcript-hash queries. Let \(I\) be the supremum absolute difference of output-1 probabilities over the same adversary class when the adversary additionally receives the real key or an independent uniform 256-bit string. Let \(\delta\) bound the increase of each of \(R,I\) when the transcript random oracle is replaced by the concrete SHA-256 role, at the same work/query budgets.

\[R\le\min\{1,2^{-256}+Q\varepsilon+\delta\},\qquad I\le\min\{1,Q\varepsilon+\delta\}.\]

Let \(\varepsilon\) bound the greatest success probability at work \(T'\) of the following task: from \((p,q,g,M,g^x,g^r)\), recovering \(g^{xr}\) for independent uniform \(x,r\in\{1,\ldots,M\}\), with the configuration's certified group parameters. The budget \(T'\) covers the adversary, lazy-hash bookkeeping, canonical transcript/element parsing and extracting one of at most \(Q\) candidate hash queries; it is not restricted to generic-group operations.

No decapsulation, key-checking or leakage oracle is available. The bounds concern a single classical target; they do not assert CCA, quantum or multi-target security. The success/advantage bounds and hash-transfer slack are explicit parameters, not numerically certified small values.

statements.label: Correctness claim
statements.title: Honest key agreement
statements.definition:

The claim is \(\Pr[K'\ne K]\le d\), averaged over the honest keys and encapsulation randomness, with \(d=0\) for every allowed exponent pair.

These are mathematical statements about the specified algorithms. They exclude invalid inputs, entropy or implementation faults, runtime aborts and side channels; they do not certify native executable correctness.

readable_sections.body:
For this stage, \(X=g^x\), \(C=g^r\), and \(Z=g^{xr}\), with independent uniform \(x,r\in\{1,\ldots,M\}\). This exact short-exponent distribution matters.

readable_sections.title: Every honest pair agrees
readable_sections.body:
The certified parameters give a prime-order subgroup, and \(1\le x,r\le M<q\). Its nonzero exponents ensure valid nonidentity public values and shared element. For every such pair,
\[
 (g^x)^r=(g^r)^x\pmod p.
\]
Encapsulation and decapsulation encode the same profile, parameters, public key, ciphertext and shared element, so their SHA-256 inputs are identical. Honest disagreement is exactly zero in this mathematical experiment. No hardness or random-oracle premise is needed; deterministic hashing is enough. Full text checks the certificate, range and encoding steps. This is not a proof of fault-free execution or side-channel resistance.

readable_sections.title: Interval computational Diffie–Hellman
readable_sections.body:
### Use in this construction

For each release-7 profile \(j\), fix its certified \((p_j,q_j,g_j)\) and set \(M_j=\min\{q_j-1,2^{\lceil2b_j+32\rceil}-1\}\), where \(b_j\) is the immutable six-decimal reference value used by `exponent_upper_bound`. The key and encapsulation exponents are independent uniform integers from \(1\) through \(M_j\). Instantiate \(T=T'\) and \(\varepsilon=\varepsilon_j\) in the Full text reduction; \(T'\) includes oracle simulation and extraction. The frozen reference defines this sampler, not a security theorem. Public group parameters remain fixed across instances.

### Scope and qualifications

Here \(T\) counts complete classical bit-RAM work, including preparation charged to this target; no uncharged secret advice or precomputed table is supplied. The probability includes the sampled inputs and the algorithm's coins. The claim is a finite-resource bound for the stated parameters, not an assertion that every small parameter choice is secure. A numerical guarantee requires an explicit \(T\) and \(\varepsilon\); none is established merely by writing the premise.

This is interval-CDH, not ordinary full-range CDH and not a discrete-logarithm premise. Computing either logarithm solves the task, but hardness of discrete logarithms alone does not establish hardness of CDH. [Shoup, section 14.1](https://www.shoup.net/papers/iso-2_1.pdf) defines ordinary CDH; the interval distribution here is an explicit variation taken from the exact sampler. The Full text proof retains its \(Q\)-query extraction loss and its separate concrete-hash premise. Honest correctness follows from group algebra and the checked parameter certificates; it needs neither hardness nor a random-oracle premise.

readable_sections.title: Random-oracle transfer for transcript hashing
readable_sections.body:
### Use in this construction

Here \(h=\mathrm{SHA256}\). Draw the interval-DH transcript \(\tau=(j,p,q,g,X,C)\) with \(X=g^x\), \(C=g^y\), \(Z=g^{xy}\) and the exact independent interval sampler above. The domain is `crucible/teaching-dh-kem/v7/shared-secret` followed by a zero byte. Frame, in order, the profile ASCII and \(p,q,g,X,C,Z\); each integer uses \(\lceil\operatorname{bitlen}(p)/8\rceil\) big-endian bytes and each field has a four-byte big-endian length prefix. This defines \(D_j,F_j\); substitute \(\delta=\delta_j\). The Full text bound remains \(\min\{1,2^{-256}+Q\varepsilon_j+\delta_j\}\) for recovery and \(\min\{1,Q\varepsilon_j+\delta_j\}\) for distinguishing.

### Scope and qualifications

The work budget includes preparation charged to one target. Every classical hash query, including pre-challenge queries, counts toward \(Q\), and its length is bounded by \(B\); the resource convention is the one fixed in Full text. In the ideal experiment the challenger and attacker use the same random function; fixed public parameters and release-identification hashes are not randomized. There is no decapsulation/equality oracle, leakage, quantum query or multi-target claim.

This is an experiment-specific modeling premise. No numerical \(\delta\) has been proved or measured; setting it to zero is an idealization. It is not a claim that a known fixed function is indistinguishable from a random oracle by direct comparison, nor a consequence of collision resistance. [Canetti, Goldreich and Halevi](https://arxiv.org/abs/cs/0010019) show why a random-oracle proof does not generally justify a concrete instantiation. The present note's ideal-hash reduction is an adaptation, not an imported concrete-SHA-256 theorem. The honest-correctness proof requires only deterministic hashing and does not use this premise.

readable_sections.title: One common measure of attack work

The plotted quantity is \(\log_2 W\), where \(W\) bounds a specified strategy's work and its stated assumptions imply at least **50% probability of recovering the complete shared key**. These are reproducible **baseline upper bounds**, not the cheapest known attacks or a security lower bound. A bigger value does not establish a more secure scheme. Full text contains the cost rules, proofs, parameter table and reproduction commands.

readable_sections.body:
Baby-step–giant-step searches the actual published exponent interval. It recovers the recipient exponent, computes the shared group element, and applies the scheme's exact transcript hash. The displayed work is a conservative upper bound with success one for honest inputs. No random-walk assumption is needed. The large table is explicitly included. This is a reproducible baseline, not the cheapest known finite-field attack; number-field-sieve and reusable-precomputation improvements are absent.

For an exponent interval \(1\le x\le M\), the table has \(m=\lceil\sqrt{M+1}\rceil\) entries. The work includes building and sorting it, every lookup and the final shared-key derivation.

rsa-kem@4.summary: Fifty configurations use certified balanced factors and a custom transcript KDF. Correctness covers every residue; factoring estimates do not establish confidentiality.

sections.title: From RSA inversion to key secrecy
sections.body:
The exact generator emits \(N=pq\); encapsulation draws \(z\) uniformly from all of \(\mathbb Z_N\), publishes \(c=z^{65537}\bmod N\), and hashes the framed transcript with \(z\).

If unit-RSA inversion for this emitted-key distribution succeeds with probability at most \(\varepsilon_j\) at the reduction's budget, then
\[
 \Pr[\text{recover the complete key}]\le2^{-256}+\varepsilon_j+\rho_j+\delta_j,
\]
where \(\rho_j=\mathbb E[1/p+1/q-1/(pq)]\) bounds the nonunit samples and \(\delta_j\) is the concrete-hash transfer allowance. Key-distinguishing advantage omits the \(2^{-256}\) term; all bounds are capped at one. Full text gives the exact reduction and a public upper bound on \(\rho_j\).

No numeric inversion hardness is asserted. The result is a classical one-challenge statement without decapsulation/equality queries, not IND-CCA or RFC 9690 compliance.

sections.title: What the inversion reduction establishes
sections.body: The scoped argument now appears in Security and Full text. It works with the actual successful structured-key distribution and all-residue encapsulation sampler, separates the nonunit probability, and accounts for the custom transcript hash. It does not establish factoring equivalence, a numeric hardness level, IND-CCA or resistance to variable-time leakage.

sections.title: Agreement includes zero and nonunit inputs
sections.body:
Successful key generation gives distinct certified primes \(p,q\) and \(ed\equiv1\pmod{(p-1)(q-1)}\). For every \(z\in\{0,\ldots,N-1\}\), including multiples of either prime,
\[
 (z^e)^d\equiv z\pmod p,\qquad (z^e)^d\equiv z\pmod q.
\]
The Chinese remainder theorem therefore gives the original \(z\) modulo \(N\). Both sides use the same fixed-width encodings and transcript hash, so honest disagreement is zero after successful bounded generation. Generation may abort; that availability issue is separate. No RSA-hardness or random-oracle premise is needed for agreement.

sections.title: What the factoring curve measures
sections.body:
For modulus bit length \(n\), the frozen classical reference is
\[
\min\{n/4,\;128F(n)/F(3072)\},\qquad
F(n)=(n\ln2)^{1/3}[\ln(n\ln2)]^{2/3}.
\]
The first term approximates rho factoring for balanced factors; the second is a normalized NFS shape. ECM, quadratic sieve, specialized attacks and constants are omitted. Small-parameter values are especially rough. The conventional 3072-bit anchor does not validate this structured generator or establish full-KEM security.

This normalized asymptotic shape is not a complete finite-parameter algorithm and success/cost analysis. Its heuristic dependencies have not been individually formalized in this note; an empty labelled-premise list does not make the estimate unconditional.

sections.title: Scope of the factoring comparison
sections.body:
The curve reports selected rho/NFS factoring approximations for this structured distribution of balanced moduli. Memory, preprocessing and success accounting limit what can be inferred from those values. The present material does not isolate a sufficiently precise additional premise to label here.

A faster algorithm or exploitable structure could lower the best known recovery cost without invalidating the cost claimed for a different attack. Neither estimate alone establishes hardness of RSA inversion or security of the full KEM. New attack evidence should identify the exact profile, algorithm, success conditions, resource units and actual dependencies.

sections.title: Quantum factoring is unpriced here
sections.body: Shor's algorithm gives a polynomial-time factoring route on a sufficiently capable quantum computer; the transcript key can then be computed. This page supplies no configuration-specific quantum circuit or physical execution budget. No numerical quantum point follows from the classical curve.

sections.title: RSA inversion
sections.body:
Fix an explicitly specified public-key distribution \(D\), supported on \((N,e)\) with \(N=pq\) for distinct primes and \(\gcd(e,(p-1)(q-1))=1\). Draw \((N,e)\leftarrow D\) and \(z\leftarrow\mathbb Z_N^*\) uniformly; set \(c=z^e\bmod N\). Given only \((N,e,c)\), the task is to recover \(z\). The RSA-inversion premise at budget \(T\) is: every classical algorithm \(A\) using at most \(T\) bit operations, including preparation, satisfies \(\Pr[A(N,e,c)=z]\le\varepsilon\). The factorization is not supplied; the probability includes key generation, the uniform unit and the algorithm's coins.

### Use in this construction

Set \(e=65537\). For profile \(j\), \(D_j\) is the law of the public key emitted by the exact bounded `rsa_v4.py` generator, conditional on successful generation in the specified execution environment. It samples certified primes of lengths \(\lceil L_j/2\rceil\) and \(\lfloor L_j/2\rfloor\), requires distinct factors and exactly \(L_j\) modulus bits, and rejects factors incompatible with \(e\). The recursive sampler constructs larger candidates as \(2Rq'+1\) from a certified prime \(q'\), with the stated Pocklington checks; it has a shared candidate budget, pair-attempt limit and deadline. This is not the uniform distribution on balanced RSA primes. The exact sampler and successful-generation conditioning are part of \(D_j\), and cannot be dropped from a faithful statement.

The actual encapsulation draws \(z\) uniformly from all of \(\mathbb Z_N\), whereas this premise concerns units. The Full text proof keeps the difference explicit: it adds \(\rho_j=\mathbb E_{D_j}[1/p+1/q-1/(pq)]\). Instantiate \(T=T'\) and \(\varepsilon=\varepsilon_j\); the candidate-verification and oracle-simulation costs are included in \(T'\).

### Scope and qualifications

Here \(T\) counts complete classical bit-RAM work, including preparation charged to this target; no uncharged secret advice or precomputed table is supplied. The probability includes the sampled inputs and the algorithm's coins. The claim is a finite-resource bound for the stated parameters, not an assertion that every small parameter choice is secure. A numerical guarantee requires an explicit \(T\) and \(\varepsilon\); none is established merely by writing the premise.

[RSA inversion in the Handbook of Applied Cryptography, section 3.3](https://cacr.uwaterloo.ca/hac/about/chap3.pdf) supplies the standard problem; \(D_j\) is the explicit implementation-specific key distribution needed here. Factoring is a sufficient attack, not a proved equivalence to inversion. [RFC 9690](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9690.html) describes an RSA-KEM with an all-residue secret sampler, but its standardized construction does not certify the security of this custom framed hash. No small-stage bound on \(\varepsilon_j\) is asserted. Honest correctness for every residue, including zero and nonunits, follows by Fermat's theorem and CRT after successful valid key generation; it does not require the inversion or hash-transfer premise.

sections.title: Random-oracle transfer for transcript hashing
sections.body:
Fix a joint distribution \(D\) of a public transcript \(\tau\) and a hidden value \(Z\), and a public encoding \(F(\tau,Z)\) injective in \(Z\). Let \(K=h(F(\tau,Z))\in\{0,1\}^{256}\). Write \(R_h\) for the best probability of recovering all of \(K\) from \(\tau\), and \(I_h\) for the best absolute difference between output-1 probabilities given \((\tau,K)\) or \((\tau,U_{256})\). Both range over classical attackers with the same stated work and hash-query budgets, without a decryption oracle. Define \(R_H,I_H\) by replacing the transcript hash with a shared random oracle \(H\). The transfer premise is \(R_h\le R_H+\delta\) and \(I_h\le I_H+\delta\).

### Use in this construction

Here \(h=\mathrm{SHA256}\). Draw \((N,e)\) from the exact successful-generation distribution \(D_j\), then \(z\) uniformly from all residues \(0,\ldots,N-1\). The public transcript contains the profile, \(N,e,c=z^e\bmod N\); the hidden value is \(Z=z\). The domain is `crucible/rsa-kem/v4/shared-secret` followed by a zero byte. The exact `rsa_v4.py` KDF length-frames the profile and canonical integer encodings of \(N,e,c,z\); those bytes, not an interchangeable RSA-KEM KDF, define \(F_j\). Substitute \(\delta=\delta_j\). The Full text retains the separate nonunit term \(\rho_j\): recovery is bounded by \(\min\{1,2^{-256}+\varepsilon_j+\rho_j+\delta_j\}\), and distinguishing by \(\min\{1,\varepsilon_j+\rho_j+\delta_j\}\).

### Scope and qualifications

The work budget includes preparation charged to one target. Every classical hash query, including pre-challenge queries, counts toward \(Q\), and its length is bounded by \(B\); the resource convention is the one fixed in Full text. In the ideal experiment the challenger and attacker use the same random function; fixed public parameters and release-identification hashes are not randomized. There is no decapsulation/equality oracle, leakage, quantum query or multi-target claim.

This is an experiment-specific modeling premise. No numerical \(\delta\) has been proved or measured; setting it to zero is an idealization. It is not a claim that a known fixed function is indistinguishable from a random oracle by direct comparison, nor a consequence of collision resistance. [Canetti, Goldreich and Halevi](https://arxiv.org/abs/cs/0010019) show why a random-oracle proof does not generally justify a concrete instantiation. The present note's ideal-hash reduction is an adaptation, not an imported concrete-SHA-256 theorem. The honest-correctness proof requires only deterministic hashing and does not use this premise.

sections.title: One common measure of attack work
sections.body:
These curves use **Classical bit-RAM v1**: elementary Boolean operations and one-bit memory transfers share a fixed accounting rule. All attack setup is charged to one fresh challenge. Memory capacity is unlimited in this abstraction, and the storage bound remains visible beside the graph.

The plotted quantity is \(\log_2 W\), where \(W\) bounds a specified strategy's work and its stated assumptions imply at least **50% probability of recovering the complete shared key**. These are reproducible **baseline upper bounds**, not the cheapest known attacks or a security lower bound. A bigger value does not establish a more secure scheme. Full text contains the cost rules, proofs, parameter table and reproduction commands.

sections.title: Trial-division recovery baseline
sections.body: This deliberately elementary baseline tries every odd candidate for the smaller certified RSA factor, reconstructs the private exponent, and recovers the encapsulated integer and transcript hash. It is guaranteed on honest inputs. It is substantially slower than established factoring attacks, including Pollard rho and the number field sieve. A high point on this curve is therefore not evidence of strong RSA security. Its purpose is to provide a complete, reproducible RAM accounting baseline until better factoring analyses have been admitted under the same model.

## Reproducible bit-RAM attack analysis

## Shared computation model: crucible-bit-ram-v1

The program is uniform in public configuration inputs; no answer-dependent
advice is permitted. Its fixed-address bit registers support arbitrary Boolean
functions of one or two bits at unit cost. Constants, fixed wiring and fixed bit
permutations are free. A dynamically addressed bit read or write costs one;
computing that address is additional charged arithmetic. This is a bit-RAM
abstraction inspired by NIST's classical gate-count discussions, not the CAT
pure circuit metric and not a NIST-approved scheme classification.

The baseline has no memory-cap constraint. It measures neither physical latency
nor energy. A pointer of b bits must be manipulated with the b-bit arithmetic
account. Loops use a public counter width and charge increment/comparison.
Input generation for the honest challenger is outside the attack budget; all
attacker initialization, candidate generation, verification and key derivation
are inside. Randomness and any rejection sampling need explicit budgets or
their own success-loss treatment. A counter on high-level Python operations is
validation of the operation census, not a trace of exact elementary gates.

Primitive upper bounds, for width w: ADD/SUB/CMP=8w; MUX=3w;
MODADD=24(w+1); MUL=16(w+1)^2; DIVMOD=64(w+1)^2;
MODMUL=80(w+1)^2; LOOP(b)=16(b+1).
MODPOW(w,e)=e(2 MODMUL(w)+MUX(w)+LOOP(e))+2w.
All bounds refer to schoolbook/ripple, restoring-division and double-and-add
algorithms. They deliberately upper-bound a particular implementation.

SHA-256/SHA-512 follow FIPS180-4. The schedule uses two small sigmas and three
word additions per expanded word. Each round uses two large sigmas, Ch, Maj,
and seven additions. Eight final additions update the chaining value. Padding
and block input/output are charged. SHA3/SHAKE follow FIPS202: Keccak-f[1600]
uses at most193536 Boolean operations (24 rounds of8064), padded to200000
for control. Absorption and output transfers are additional. These are
algorithmic upper bounds, not claims about optimized hardware.

Every profile's complete attack is stopped within its reported budget. Its
success statement names the probability space and any unproved premises.
The resulting curve is a documented attack upper bound, not a proven security
level and not necessarily the cheapest known attack. No 50%-success result is
inferred simply by dividing cost by average success probability.

Primary specifications:
- https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/FIPS/NIST.FIPS.180-4.pdf
- https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/FIPS/NIST.FIPS.202.pdf


## Reproduction

From this source checkout:
```text
python scripts/build_ram_attack_notes.py --check
python -m pytest tests/test_ram_common.py tests/test_ram_classical_attacks.py tests/test_ram_lattice_attacks.py tests/test_ram_code_attacks.py tests/test_ram_catalogue.py
```
The generated `crucible/data/ram_attack_curves.json` retains integer cost components, parameters, assumptions and source-file hashes. No cryptographic-size attack is executed. Small examples check implementation paths; they do not verify heuristic premises at large sizes. No external model service or paid API is used.

## Trial-division recovery baseline

Worked configuration: rsa-v4-tier-50. The same algorithm and parameterized formulas generate the other rows below.

For an n-bit modulus the adapter samples a factor q of exactly k=floor(n/2) bits. All such factors are odd. Try every d=2^(k-1)+1,2^(k-1)+3,...,2^k-1. There are exactly 2^(k-2) candidates. Restoring binary division finds q (or another prime factor) with certainty, independent of the nonuniform Pocklington sampler. Set p=N/q and phi=(p-1)(q-1). To avoid an unaccounted large-integer inverse, exploit the fixed prime e=65537: set u=(phi mod e)^(e-2) mod e and t=(-u) mod e. Then d=(1+t*phi)/e is an integer with ed=1 mod phi and d<phi. The sampler enforces gcd(e,phi)=1. Compute z=c^d mod N, including z that is not a unit; Fermat and CRT prove recovery for every honest z. Verify z^e=c, then apply the exact framed 1223-byte SHA-256 transcript. All primitive costs and loop control are charged; O(n) workspace suffices. This upper bound is neither a best-known factoring estimate nor a hardness premise.

Success statement for this worked configuration: 1

rsa-kem@4.full_text_argument_appendix:
## Exact-release security and correctness argument

### Exact experiment and meaning of the claim

Fix one registered profile j, the published construction and all exact parameter bytes. Key generation emits a fresh honest public key; encapsulation emits one ciphertext C and a 256-bit key K. The public transcript includes the profile and parameters. The recovery adversary receives this transcript, not K, and outputs one 256-bit candidate; success means equality with **the entire key**, never recovery of half its bits. A participant's multiple guesses or multiple target instances require a separately counted game. The one-challenge distinguishing adversary additionally receives either K or an independent uniform 256-bit string. Its advantage is the absolute difference of its probability of outputting 1 in those two experiments, with no factor-of-two convention hidden in the definition. Neither adversary receives a decapsulation oracle, a correctness/equality oracle, private state or timing leakage. Public encapsulation can be performed by the adversary itself within its budget.

The theorem below concerns classical algorithms and classical oracle queries. T counts the complete attack work, including preparation charged to this target; Q bounds all hash queries, including those made before the challenge is supplied; B bounds their bit length. Public fixed parameters may be known before the challenge, but uncharged secret advice or a precomputed discrete-log table is not granted. Multi-target amortization is a different resource statement. These are finite-parameter success relations, not an asymptotic assertion that all 50 small and large stages are secure.

Write F(T_pub,Z) for the adapter's exact domain-separated, length-framed KDF input. In the ideal experiment the transcript KDF uses a uniformly random function H from bitstrings to 256-bit strings, shared consistently between challenger and adversary. Fixed release-identification hashes and public parameters remain public inputs; they are not re-randomized artifact identities. The public prefix is fixed by T_pub and the final encoded secret is injective. Let Hit mean that the adversary asks H at F(T_pub,Z).

### Why the exact-query event controls success

Lazy-sample H: keep a table, give a new independent uniform answer to each new input, and reuse it on repeats. If Hit never occurs, the value H(F(T_pub,Z)) has never been shown. Even conditioned on the whole non-Hit transcript and the adversary's output, that value remains uniform and independent. Therefore complete-key recovery has probability at most Pr[Hit] + 2^(-256). Collisions with another oracle output do not need a separate birthday term: an unseen target output is still uniform, and accidental equality is included in 2^(-256).

For distinguishing, compare the real-key game with a game that gives an independent uniform test key. Couple their coins and all oracle replies until the first target-input query. Before that query their distributions agree, including pre-challenge queries; if a target-input query already occurred, mark Hit before revealing the test key. Thus the difference of output-1 probabilities is at most Pr[Hit] in the independent-test-key game. That game is simulatable without knowing Z. The reductions below bound its Hit probability as well as recovery's Hit probability.

The lazy-oracle simulator can use a simple list, so its bookkeeping is at most O(Q^2(B+256)) bit operations and O(Q(B+256)) bits of memory, plus the explicitly stated extraction arithmetic and the adversary's work. This deliberately loose bound makes the reduction executable without treating hash-table lookup as a free operation. It is not a plotted concrete attack-cost estimate. An implementation with better lookup can tighten it; no numeric security level is inferred from the O notation.

### Concrete hash transfer and what has actually been proved

The random-oracle theorem is a mathematical statement in that model. For the implemented SHA-256 KDF, a separate premise specifies an additive transfer slack delta: for the declared adversary/resource class, real complete-key recovery is no more than the ideal recovery plus delta, and real distinguishing advantage is no more than ideal advantage plus delta. This premise applies to the exact framed-input construction, not to every use of SHA-256. It does not assert that a fixed public hash is indistinguishable from a random oracle under a naive direct comparison; such an assertion would be false. No bound on delta has been proved or measured here. Setting delta=0 is the usual ideal-model extrapolation, explicitly an assumption. Collision resistance alone does not supply this premise.

The reductions and algebra below are locally authored derivations. The cited literature supplies their lineage and relevant standard constructions, not an independent approval of this implementation. We have not proved source-code refinement, constant-time behavior, resistance to malformed inputs, multi-session security or IND-CCA. No one-hour limit or current attack plot is turned into a lower bound by these arguments.

### Exact RSA distribution and framing

At stage j, the fixed modulus bit length L determines factor lengths ceil(L/2) and floor(L/2). The generator recursively samples certified primes using p=2Rq+1 and base-2 Pocklington witnesses, rejects factors with gcd(65537,p-1)!=1, rejects equal factors and wrong-width products, and enforces candidate, pair-attempt and runtime limits. Let D_j be the distribution of successfully emitted keys in the specified generation environment. The theorem is conditional on generation success, for that actual D_j; it makes neither a uniform-prime assertion nor a bound on abort probability. Runtime conditioning may bias D_j and is included in its definition.

The public key is the L-width modulus followed by exactly three bytes 01 00 01. With w=ceil(L/8), the ciphertext and z each use w big-endian bytes. The KDF input is domain `crucible/rsa-kem/v4/shared-secret\0`, then length-framed profile ASCII, N bytes, e bytes, c bytes and z bytes. For a fixed public transcript it is injective in z. The exponentiation map is a permutation on all Z_N, as the correctness proof below shows. Consequently each canonical c identifies exactly one z, even when z is not a unit.

### Recovery and distinguishing reduction, including nonunits

Let S_j^unit(T') denote the best success at inverting c=z^e mod N for N sampled from D_j and independent uniform z in Z_N*, within budget T'. A reduction receives N,e,c from this unit inversion experiment and runs the adversary with a lazy random oracle (plus an independent uniform test key for a distinguishing adversary). It exposes only N,e during any pre-challenge phase and withholds c and the test key until the challenge phase; all earlier queries are recorded and count toward Q. On every query whose framing and public prefix match the target, parse a canonical z candidate in [0,N-1] and test z^65537 mod N=c. The map is bijective, so a passing candidate is exactly the target preimage. The solver stops and returns it. Thus on unit targets the target-input query event is bounded by S_j^unit(T') with **no Q factor in success loss**.

The reduction performs at most Q public-exponent checks. Each requires 16 squarings and one multiplication with a left-to-right binary implementation of e=2^16+1, plus input parsing and comparison. With schoolbook modular arithmetic this adds O(Q*L^2) bit work to the lazy-oracle bookkeeping. This overhead belongs in T'; it is not free. No factorization or private key is supplied to the reduction.

Actual encapsulation samples all z in Z_N. For each fixed emitted key the probability of a nonunit is exactly
\[
 \rho(N)=1-\frac{(p-1)(q-1)}{pq}=\frac1p+\frac1q-\frac1{pq}.
\]
Average this over D_j to obtain rho_j. On unit inputs, weight each fixed-key Hit probability by at most one; averaging is bounded by the inversion experiment with the same D_j and a uniform unit. On nonunit inputs, pessimistically bound the entire event by rho_j. This avoids silently changing the modulus distribution when conditioning a joint experiment on the unit event. Therefore Pr[Hit] <= S_j^unit(T')+rho_j.

Combining with the exact-query lemma gives
\[
 P_{\mathrm{recover}}^{\mathrm{RO}}\le\min\{1,2^{-256}+S_j^{\rm unit}(T')+\rho_j\},\qquad
 \operatorname{Adv}_{\mathrm{key}}^{\mathrm{RO}}\le\min\{1,S_j^{\rm unit}(T')+\rho_j\}.
\]
If the inversion premise gives S_j^unit(T')<=epsilon_j, substitute it; add the explicitly assumed delta_j to transfer to the concrete KDF. Alternatively one can formulate full-domain RSA inversion and omit rho_j, but then that hardness premise itself includes the easy nonunit cases. We use the familiar unit-domain statement and make its loss visible.

The fixed factor lengths give a public, distribution-independent upper bound
\[
 \rho_j < 2^{1-\lceil L/2\rceil}+2^{1-\lfloor L/2\rfloor}.
\]
At L=32 this is 2^(-14); at L=3072 it is 2^(-1534). These are upper bounds on a sampling term, not total security estimates. Nonunit cases really can be easy: c=0 implies z=0; if 1<gcd(c,N)<N, the gcd yields a factor, enabling inversion. This phenomenon affects secrecy but never invalidates honest correctness. A small epsilon_j at a small stage must not be presumed.

### Complete honest-correctness argument

Prime certificates recurse to exact trial division and use Pocklington's criterion at larger nodes. For n=2Rq+1 with certified q>sqrt(n), the Fermat/gcd witnesses force q to divide ell-1 for every prime divisor ell of n; hence all such divisors exceed sqrt(n), proving n prime. Successful key generation therefore gives distinct primes p,q. The filter makes e coprime to both p-1 and q-1, and hence to phi(N); d is the multiplicative inverse modulo phi(N).

For any z in [0,N-1], if z=0 mod p then z^(ed)=z=0 mod p. Otherwise Fermat and ed=1+k(p-1)(q-1) imply z^(ed)=z mod p. The same two cases apply modulo q. Distinct primes are coprime, so CRT yields z^(ed)=z mod N. This includes z=0, multiples of p or q, and every unit. The result lies in [0,N-1], so its fixed-width byte encoding equals the original z encoding. Decapsulation reconstructs N and e and preserves the exact canonical ciphertext, giving identical framed hash inputs and equal outputs. No collision-resistance or secrecy premise enters this proof.

The general algebra proves zero disagreement for the specified honest operations, conditional on successful valid generation. A failed generation attempt produces no challenge and is not a decryption failure. Variable-time code, side channels and hardware faults are outside the experiment. Conformance tests cover real stage-1/25/50 keys, including forced nonunit targets; the independent exhaustive residue check illustrates the CRT and permutation claims on four small test moduli. Neither finite test is a formal verification of the Python implementation.

statements.label: Security claim
statements.title: Passive key recovery and distinguishing
statements.definition:
For every registered native configuration of exact research release `rsa-kem@4`, generate one fresh honest public key and one encapsulation. Let R be the supremum probability, among classical adversaries using at most T total computation work and the stated query budgets, of returning the complete 256-bit shared key in one output. Probability includes honest generation, encapsulation and the adversary's coins; condition on valid successful generation. Pre-challenge computation and designated hash queries count toward the same budgets.

Let \(Q\) bound transcript-hash queries. Let \(I\) be the supremum absolute difference of output-1 probabilities over the same adversary class when the adversary additionally receives the real key or an independent uniform 256-bit string. Let \(\delta\) bound the increase of each of \(R,I\) when the transcript random oracle is replaced by the concrete SHA-256 role, at the same work/query budgets.

\[R\le\min\{1,2^{-256}+\varepsilon+\rho+\delta\},\qquad I\le\min\{1,\varepsilon+\rho+\delta\}.\]

Let \(\varepsilon\) bound the greatest success probability, at work \(T'\), of recovering a uniform \(z\in\mathbb Z_N^*\) from \((N,65537,z^{65537}\bmod N)\), for the exact bounded generator's emitted-key distribution. Let \(\rho=\mathbb E[1/p+1/q-1/(pq)]\) over those emitted keys \(N=pq\). The budget \(T'\) covers the adversary, lazy-hash bookkeeping and at most \(Q\) canonical parsing/public exponentiation checks.

No decapsulation, key-checking or leakage oracle is available. The bounds concern a single classical target; they do not assert CCA, quantum or multi-target security. The success/advantage bounds and hash-transfer slack are explicit parameters, not numerically certified small values.

statements.label: Correctness claim
statements.title: Honest key agreement
statements.definition:
For every registered native configuration of exact research release `rsa-kem@4`, run honest \((pk,sk)\leftarrow\mathsf{KeyGen}\), \((C,K)\leftarrow\mathsf{Encaps}(pk)\) and \(K'=\mathsf{Decaps}(sk,C)\) using its specified samplers, mathematical algorithms, exact arithmetic and canonical encodings. Condition on valid successful key generation and completed operations, never on agreement.

The claim is \(\Pr[K'\ne K]\le d\), averaged over the honest keys and encapsulation randomness, with \(d=0\) for every \(z\in\mathbb Z_N\), including zero and nonunits.

These are mathematical statements about the specified algorithms. They exclude invalid inputs, entropy or implementation faults, runtime aborts and side channels; they do not certify native executable correctness.

statements.label: Reference claim
statements.title: What the factoring curve measures — stated conclusion
statements.definition:
**Unquantified reference.** For modulus bit length \(n\), the frozen classical reference is
\[
\min\{n/4,\;128F(n)/F(3072)\},\qquad
F(n)=(n\ln2)^{1/3}[\ln(n\ln2)]^{2/3}.
\]
The first term approximates rho factoring for balanced factors; the second is a normalized NFS shape. ECM, quadratic sieve, specialized attacks and constants are omitted. Small-parameter values are especially rough. The conventional 3072-bit anchor does not validate this structured generator or establish full-KEM security.

This normalized asymptotic shape is not a complete finite-parameter algorithm and success/cost analysis. Its heuristic dependencies have not been individually formalized in this note; an empty labelled-premise list does not make the estimate unconditional.

**Scope.** Exact research release rsa-kem@4; classical model classical-baseline-v2 (heuristic-reference). Retain the source's qualifications; this is not converted into a current comparable bit-RAM estimate. This entry does not supply a complete quantified attack guarantee in the common computation model.

readable_sections.title: From RSA inversion to key secrecy
readable_sections.body:
The exact generator emits \(N=pq\); encapsulation draws \(z\) uniformly from all of \(\mathbb Z_N\), publishes \(c=z^{65537}\bmod N\), and hashes the framed transcript with \(z\).

If unit-RSA inversion for this emitted-key distribution succeeds with probability at most \(\varepsilon_j\) at the reduction's budget, then
\[
 \Pr[\text{recover the complete key}]\le2^{-256}+\varepsilon_j+\rho_j+\delta_j,
\]
where \(\rho_j=\mathbb E[1/p+1/q-1/(pq)]\) bounds the nonunit samples and \(\delta_j\) is the concrete-hash transfer allowance. Key-distinguishing advantage omits the \(2^{-256}\) term; all bounds are capped at one. Full text gives the exact reduction and a public upper bound on \(\rho_j\).

No numeric inversion hardness is asserted. The result is a classical one-challenge statement without decapsulation/equality queries, not IND-CCA or RFC 9690 compliance.

readable_sections.title: What the inversion reduction establishes
readable_sections.body: The scoped argument now appears in Security and Full text. It works with the actual successful structured-key distribution and all-residue encapsulation sampler, separates the nonunit probability, and accounts for the custom transcript hash. It does not establish factoring equivalence, a numeric hardness level, IND-CCA or resistance to variable-time leakage.

readable_sections.title: Agreement includes zero and nonunit inputs
readable_sections.body:
Successful key generation gives distinct certified primes \(p,q\) and \(ed\equiv1\pmod{(p-1)(q-1)}\). For every \(z\in\{0,\ldots,N-1\}\), including multiples of either prime,
\[
 (z^e)^d\equiv z\pmod p,\qquad (z^e)^d\equiv z\pmod q.
\]
The Chinese remainder theorem therefore gives the original \(z\) modulo \(N\). Both sides use the same fixed-width encodings and transcript hash, so honest disagreement is zero after successful bounded generation. Generation may abort; that availability issue is separate. No RSA-hardness or random-oracle premise is needed for agreement.

\]
The first term approximates rho factoring for balanced factors; the second is a normalized NFS shape. ECM, quadratic sieve, specialized attacks and constants are omitted. Small-parameter values are especially rough. The conventional 3072-bit anchor does not validate this structured generator or establish full-KEM security.

readable_sections.body:

A faster algorithm or exploitable structure could lower the best known recovery cost without invalidating the cost claimed for a different attack. Neither estimate alone establishes hardness of RSA inversion or security of the full KEM. readable_sections.title: RSA inversion
readable_sections.body:
### Use in this construction

Set \(e=65537\). For profile \(j\), \(D_j\) is the law of the public key emitted by the exact bounded `rsa_v4.py` generator, conditional on successful generation in the specified execution environment. It samples certified primes of lengths \(\lceil L_j/2\rceil\) and \(\lfloor L_j/2\rfloor\), requires distinct factors and exactly \(L_j\) modulus bits, and rejects factors incompatible with \(e\). The recursive sampler constructs larger candidates as \(2Rq'+1\) from a certified prime \(q'\), with the stated Pocklington checks; it has a shared candidate budget, pair-attempt limit and deadline. This is not the uniform distribution on balanced RSA primes. The exact sampler and successful-generation conditioning are part of \(D_j\), and cannot be dropped from a faithful statement.

The actual encapsulation draws \(z\) uniformly from all of \(\mathbb Z_N\), whereas this premise concerns units. The Full text proof keeps the difference explicit: it adds \(\rho_j=\mathbb E_{D_j}[1/p+1/q-1/(pq)]\). Instantiate \(T=T'\) and \(\varepsilon=\varepsilon_j\); the candidate-verification and oracle-simulation costs are included in \(T'\).

### Scope and qualifications

Here \(T\) counts complete classical bit-RAM work, including preparation charged to this target; no uncharged secret advice or precomputed table is supplied. The probability includes the sampled inputs and the algorithm's coins. The claim is a finite-resource bound for the stated parameters, not an assertion that every small parameter choice is secure. A numerical guarantee requires an explicit \(T\) and \(\varepsilon\); none is established merely by writing the premise.

[RSA inversion in the Handbook of Applied Cryptography, section 3.3](https://cacr.uwaterloo.ca/hac/about/chap3.pdf) supplies the standard problem; \(D_j\) is the explicit implementation-specific key distribution needed here. Factoring is a sufficient attack, not a proved equivalence to inversion. [RFC 9690](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9690.html) describes an RSA-KEM with an all-residue secret sampler, but its standardized construction does not certify the security of this custom framed hash. No small-stage bound on \(\varepsilon_j\) is asserted. Honest correctness for every residue, including zero and nonunits, follows by Fermat's theorem and CRT after successful valid key generation; it does not require the inversion or hash-transfer premise.

readable_sections.title: Random-oracle transfer for transcript hashing
readable_sections.body:
### Use in this construction

Here \(h=\mathrm{SHA256}\). Draw \((N,e)\) from the exact successful-generation distribution \(D_j\), then \(z\) uniformly from all residues \(0,\ldots,N-1\). The public transcript contains the profile, \(N,e,c=z^e\bmod N\); the hidden value is \(Z=z\). The domain is `crucible/rsa-kem/v4/shared-secret` followed by a zero byte. The exact `rsa_v4.py` KDF length-frames the profile and canonical integer encodings of \(N,e,c,z\); those bytes, not an interchangeable RSA-KEM KDF, define \(F_j\). Substitute \(\delta=\delta_j\). The Full text retains the separate nonunit term \(\rho_j\): recovery is bounded by \(\min\{1,2^{-256}+\varepsilon_j+\rho_j+\delta_j\}\), and distinguishing by \(\min\{1,\varepsilon_j+\rho_j+\delta_j\}\).

### Scope and qualifications

The work budget includes preparation charged to one target. Every classical hash query, including pre-challenge queries, counts toward \(Q\), and its length is bounded by \(B\); the resource convention is the one fixed in Full text. In the ideal experiment the challenger and attacker use the same random function; fixed public parameters and release-identification hashes are not randomized. There is no decapsulation/equality oracle, leakage, quantum query or multi-target claim.

This is an experiment-specific modeling premise. No numerical \(\delta\) has been proved or measured; setting it to zero is an idealization. It is not a claim that a known fixed function is indistinguishable from a random oracle by direct comparison, nor a consequence of collision resistance. [Canetti, Goldreich and Halevi](https://arxiv.org/abs/cs/0010019) show why a random-oracle proof does not generally justify a concrete instantiation. The present note's ideal-hash reduction is an adaptation, not an imported concrete-SHA-256 theorem. The honest-correctness proof requires only deterministic hashing and does not use this premise.

readable_sections.title: Trial-division recovery baseline

It is guaranteed on honest inputs. It is substantially slower than established factoring attacks, including Pollard rho and the number field sieve. A high point on this curve is therefore not evidence of strong RSA security. Its purpose is to provide a complete, reproducible RAM accounting baseline until better factoring analyses have been admitted under the same model.

sections.title: From shared-point hardness to key secrecy
sections.body:
This release uses its own certified short-Weierstrass curves, not X25519. With independent uniform nonzero scalars, \(X=xG\), \(C=rG\), and \(Z=xrG\).

If shared-point recovery at the reduction's budget has probability at most \(\varepsilon_j\), then a classical adversary making \(Q\) hash queries satisfies
\[
 \Pr[\text{recover the complete key}]\le2^{-256}+Q\varepsilon_j+\delta_j.
\]
The one-challenge key-distinguishing advantage is at most \(Q\varepsilon_j+\delta_j\); bounds are capped at one. \(\delta_j\) names the unproved transfer from the random-oracle model to the concrete hash.

Full text derives the reduction for the actual compressed encoding. It assigns no numeric hardness level and grants no decapsulation/equality oracle. Prime-order certificates and generic-rho curves alone do not prove that \(\varepsilon_j\) is small.

sections.title: What this secrecy argument covers
sections.body: Security and Full text develop a scoped passive argument for the custom curve, compressed encoding and transcript hash. It does not inherit X25519 or HPKE security claims and does not establish IND-CCA, multi-session composition or side-channel resistance.

sections.title: Every honest scalar pair agrees
sections.body:
The public certificates establish prime field and group orders. Nonzero scalars in the prime-order group produce nonidentity points, and canonical compression retains the entire point, including its sign. Therefore
\[
 r(xG)=x(rG).
\]
Both sides reconstruct identical compressed public key, ciphertext and shared-point bytes before hashing. Honest disagreement is zero for every supported scalar pair under exact arithmetic and encoding, with no cryptographic premise. Full text explains the order certificate and compression step; implementation faults, malformed inputs and timing leakage are outside this statement.

sections.title: The generic rho curve
sections.body:
The classical reference is \(\tfrac12\log_2q\): the square-root scale of generic rho search. Its unit is modeled group operations. Constants, memory, parallel tradeoffs, special curve attacks and implementation costs are omitted.

The deterministic curve search excludes specified unwanted properties. That is not an exhaustive weak-curve exclusion or a proof that rho is optimal. The generic reference is therefore not a lower bound on the best attack.

This is an asymptotic reference rather than a specified walk with a complete finite-parameter success/cost analysis. The note does not instantiate the needed analysis or isolate its hypotheses; an empty labelled-premise list does not certify an unconditional runtime guarantee.

sections.body:
The rho curve reports a generic square-root operation scale for the selected group. It does not assert that rho is the fastest attack on that curve. A faster curve-specific attack could lower the best known recovery cost without invalidating rho's own cost estimate.

The current source gives a reference scale rather than a complete success-normalized implementation analysis. It does not isolate a sufficiently precise additional premise to label here. sections.title: Elliptic-curve computational Diffie–Hellman
sections.body:
Fix a nonsingular elliptic curve \(E/\mathbb F_p\), with \(p\) prime, and a point \(P\in E(\mathbb F_p)\) of prime order \(q\). Sample \(x,y\) independently and uniformly from \(\mathbb Z_q^*\). Given \((E,P,q,xP,yP)\), the task is to output \(xyP\). The elliptic-curve CDH premise at budget \(T\) is: every classical algorithm \(A\) using at most \(T\) bit operations, including preparation, satisfies \(\Pr[A(E,P,q,xP,yP)=xyP]\le\varepsilon\). The curve and points have their concrete public encodings; the attacker is not restricted to generic group operations.

### Use in this construction

For each compressed-curve profile \(j\), substitute the certified prime-field curve and generator from `ec_parameters.json`. Its entire curve group has prime order \(q_j\); both scalars are independently uniform in \(1,\ldots,q_j-1\). Instantiate \(T=T'\) and \(\varepsilon=\varepsilon_j\) in the Full text proof, including its simulation and extraction costs. These are the registered short-Weierstrass curves: the historical scheme identifier does not make them X25519, and hardness is not inherited from a different standardized curve.

The curve is fixed, not drawn from an unspecified random-curve family. The nonzero scalar distribution is explicit; it is not silently replaced by the all-scalar convention. [Shoup, sections 13–14](https://www.shoup.net/papers/iso-2_1.pdf) provides the underlying CDH definition and finite-field/elliptic-group setting. The Full text reduction retains its \(Q\)-query loss and separate concrete-hash premise. Certificates prove primality and the group order, not CDH hardness. Honest agreement follows from the group law and injective point encoding without an unproved correctness premise.
