readable_sections.title: The hidden message behind a fresh challenge
readable_sections.body:
The native encryption core hides a uniform 128-bit message \(m\) in its quasi-cyclic noisy ciphertext. The KEM derives both the key and encryption coins from a domain-separated hash of the public-key digest, \(m\), and a public salt.

A complete passive key-recovery argument can use the exact native core’s message-recovery hardness directly. It keeps the real seeded and slightly biased samplers in that problem; it does not silently replace them with independent ideal samples. The two premises below give the precise conditional statement.

readable_sections.title: From one-way encryption to shared-key recovery
readable_sections.body:
Let \(\epsilon_{\rm PKE}(T)\) bound recovery of the uniform native message from an encryption using independent uniform coins, and let \(q_G\) bound classical queries to the key-and-coins hash. Then the stated oracle model gives
\[\Pr[\widehat K=K]\le\min\{1,q_G\epsilon_{\rm PKE}(T_B)+2^{-256}\}.\]
A reduction guesses the first oracle query containing the hidden message. Before that query, the ciphertext distribution is exactly the native one with uniform coins. Full text gives the simulation, including why it need not know the coins or test which candidate message is correct.

This passive argument supplies no numerical hardness estimate and does not instantiate the stronger CCA theorem. In particular, average honest correctness is not automatically the message-wise correctness needed by a CCA reduction.

These inequalities are in the stated oracle model. A concrete-implementation claim must add the separate hash-transfer slack \(\delta_{\rm hash}\) and cap the result at one.

readable_sections.title: Exact agreement first; a conditional tail later
readable_sections.body:
The residual after cancellation is the truncated \(xr_2+r_1y+e\), whose weight is at most \(B=2ww_r+w_e\). A wrong repeated-RM symbol needs at least \(32r\) bit errors, conservatively including ties, and the outer RS decoder corrects \(\delta\) wrong symbols. Thus
\[B<(\delta+1)32r\]
guarantees every supported honest input decodes. Stages 1–4 satisfy this inequality and have unconditional zero mathematical disagreement.

For stages 5–66, the rational certificate establishes a ceiling \(2^{-128}\) only under the two displayed correctness premises. Full text separates the exact finite calculation from the unproved transfer to concrete seeded, correlated noise. Failure of the support inequality is not itself a decoding failure.

readable_sections.title: Seed expansion does not worsen decoding
readable_sections.body:
Fix \(R=\mathbb F_2[X]/(X^n-1)\), truncation \(\pi_L\), and the specified repeated-RM/RS encoder and decoder \(E,D\). For a uniform 128-bit message and vectors with weights \(w,w,w_r,w_r,w_e\), define

\[
F(m,x,y,r_1,r_2,e)=\mathbf1\!\left[D\!\left(E(m)+\pi_L(xr_2+r_1y+e)\right)\ne m\right].
\]

This is the honest message-decoding failure event. Cancellation in the public equations gives exactly the displayed residual. Failure is averaged over honest messages and fresh keys; no supremum over maliciously chosen messages is taken. A retained decoder rejection is a failure. Native process crashes or invalid-generation operational errors are tracked separately, not discarded as successful observations.

\(\mathcal D_{\rm seed}\) is the actual finite-seed honest sampling law: it includes the public key seed, SHA3/SHAKE expansions, uniform message and salt, and the actual derivation of the encryption seed from those values. In particular it does not silently replace the concrete \(G(H(P)\Vert m\Vert z)\) encryption seed by a new independent draw. \(\mathcal D_{\rm ideal}\) replaces the declared honest expansion outputs by independent uniform expansion streams, consistently reused on repeated inputs, while retaining the same samplers, their bounds, the codec and its tie rules. The key sampler uses rejection for uniform fixed weight; the encryption sampler uses its specified fixed-work 32-bit procedure and retains that procedure's bias. No resampling is conditioned on successful decryption.

### Use in this construction

The binding is `hqc@modeled-research-v3`: 66 tuples from `crucible/data/hqc_model_profiles.json`, with \(n_1=16+2\delta\), \(1\le\delta\le15\), and \(1\le r\le3\). The fixed native source is liboqs commit `5a1a854b0dc9f2141bdc771c555ee60c37950183`, with the source/archive and specialization recorded in `docs/hqc-model-v3.txt`. Only the declared parameter headers are specialized. The construction, domain separators and seed maps retain the [2025-08-22 HQC specification](https://pqc-hqc.org/doc/hqc_specifications_2025_08_22.pdf), Sections 3.1–3.6. The 2026 specification is a different construction/parameter target and is not substituted for it.

The premise is needed only for the statistical correctness route at stages 5–66. Stages 1–4 have a separate deterministic support proof. `docs/hqc-model-v3.txt` fixes the ideal-expansion comparison and retained samplers; the authored full argument specifies the same honest failure event.

No transfer bound for the concrete expanders is proved. If evidence only supports \(\Pr_{\rm seed}[F]\le\Pr_{\rm ideal}[F]+\eta\), then \(\eta\) must remain in the final correctness bound. This premise concerns average decoding failure, not pseudorandomness against all distinguishers, the security hash transfer, or message-wise correctness required by stronger CCA arguments.

readable_sections.title: Correlated noise obeys the decoder bound
readable_sections.body:
### Use in this construction

The binding is `hqc@modeled-research-v3`: 66 tuples from `crucible/data/hqc_model_profiles.json`, with \(n_1=16+2\delta\), \(1\le\delta\le15\), and \(1\le r\le3\). The fixed native source is liboqs commit `5a1a854b0dc9f2141bdc771c555ee60c37950183`, with the source/archive and specialization recorded in `docs/hqc-model-v3.txt`. Only the declared parameter headers are specialized. The construction, domain separators and seed maps retain the [2025-08-22 HQC specification](https://pqc-hqc.org/doc/hqc_specifications_2025_08_22.pdf), Sections 3.1–3.6. The 2026 specification is a different construction/parameter target and is not substituted for it.

The premise applies to the statistical route at stages 5–66. The complete arithmetic is executable in `crucible/hqc_model_correctness.py` and pinned by each profile's certificate. It proves \(B_{\rm model}\le2^{-128}\) for those selected tuples; it does not prove the comparison \(\Pr[F]\le B_{\rm model}\).

The bound's provenance is the [2026-10-12 HQC specification](https://pqc-hqc.org/doc/hqc_specifications_2026_10_12.pdf), Sections 6.1.1–6.1.5 and 6.2.3, retaining Model 1 and the declared tie and bias corrections for this older construction. Its use on reduced tuples is an explicit unproved transfer. Actual cyclic products have correlations and fixed parity; equal marginals are insufficient, and ordinary simulation cannot certify a \(2^{-128}\) tail. A counterexample to independence alone would not refute this weaker event bound.

readable_sections.title: The earlier reference and remaining cryptanalysis
readable_sections.body:
The earlier catalogue supplied no calibrated attack-cost curve for these 66 tuples. The elementary bit-RAM attacks below now provide explicit conditional work bounds. Competitive best-known attack estimates still require further cryptanalysis.

The October 2026 specification changes weights and other construction details. The retained August 2025 release cannot inherit the newer assessment, and conditional correctness is not a confidentiality estimate. An alternative low-weight solution to one public equation need not yield the target key; each attack must include its actual success argument and final key derivation.

readable_sections.title: Seeded noisy-product message recovery
readable_sections.body:
The public parameters are \((n,w,w_r,w_e,n_1,r)\), the code \(E:\{0,1\}^{128}\to\{0,1\}^{L}\) with \(L=128rn_1\le n\), its decoder \(D\), and specified deterministic seed maps. In \(R=\mathbb F_2[X]/(X^n-1)\), addition is coefficientwise XOR and multiplication is cyclic convolution. The map \(\pi_L\) keeps the first \(L\) coefficients.

\(S_K\) maps a uniform 256-bit initial key seed to a public seed \(\alpha\) and secret vectors \(x,y\), both of weight \(w\), using the specified key-generation expansion and successful-generation rules. \(H_X(\alpha)=h\) is the public vector expansion. \(S_R(\theta)=(r_1,r_2,e)\) expands a 256-bit encryption seed, with weights \((w_r,w_r,w_e)\). These maps, including finite-seed correlations, rejection rules and sampling bias, are public parameters of the problem. They are not assumed to produce uniform independent ring elements.

The public key is \(P=(\alpha,s)\), where \(s=x+hy\). Define the core encryption map

\[
\mathcal E(P,m;\theta)=\left(r_1+hr_2,\ E(m)+\pi_L(sr_2+e)\right),\qquad (r_1,r_2,e)=S_R(\theta).
\]

The public seed \(\alpha\), not merely its expansion \(h\), is included in the attacker's input. The retained codec is an outer RS\((n_1,16)\) code over \(\mathbb F_{256}\), followed by \(r\)-fold repeated RM\((1,7)\); its field representation, coordinate order and deterministic tie rules are part of \(E,D\).

The message and both initial seeds are independent. Winning means returning the actual 128-bit message, with probability over those draws and the attacker's coins. The work budget counts all attacker preprocessing and verification. This formulation includes attacks exploiting the public seed, code, truncation, parity, ring structure or concrete expanders.

### Use in this construction

The binding is `hqc@modeled-research-v3`: 66 tuples from `crucible/data/hqc_model_profiles.json`, with \(n_1=16+2\delta\), \(1\le\delta\le15\), and \(1\le r\le3\). The fixed native source is liboqs commit `5a1a854b0dc9f2141bdc771c555ee60c37950183`, with the source/archive and specialization recorded in `docs/hqc-model-v3.txt`. Only the declared parameter headers are specialized. The construction, domain separators and seed maps retain the [2025-08-22 HQC specification](https://pqc-hqc.org/doc/hqc_specifications_2025_08_22.pdf), Sections 3.1–3.6. The 2026 specification is a different construction/parameter target and is not substituted for it.

This is the exact core one-wayness premise used by the local passive key-recovery proof. The 2025 specification's Theorem 6.2 offers a different, distinguishing route through parity-aware 2-DQCSD and truncated 3-DQCSD. No reduction from this particular finite-seed, reduced-parameter message-recovery problem to those idealized problems is supplied here. Calling it simply “syndrome decoding is hard” would hide that missing bridge. No numerical \(\epsilon_{\rm PKE}(T)\), CCA guarantee or asymptotic negligible bound is inferred.

readable_sections.body:
The public parameters are \((n,w,w_r,w_e,n_1,r)\), the code \(E:\{0,1\}^{128}\to\{0,1\}^{L}\) with \(L=128rn_1\le n\), its decoder \(D\), and specified deterministic seed maps. In \(R=\mathbb F_2[X]/(X^n-1)\), addition is coefficientwise XOR and multiplication is cyclic convolution. The map \(\pi_L\) keeps the first \(L\) coefficients.

\(S_K\) maps a uniform 256-bit initial key seed to a public seed \(\alpha\) and secret vectors \(x,y\), both of weight \(w\), using the specified key-generation expansion and successful-generation rules. \(H_X(\alpha)=h\) is the public vector expansion. \(S_R(\theta)=(r_1,r_2,e)\) expands a 256-bit encryption seed, with weights \((w_r,w_r,w_e)\). These maps, including finite-seed correlations, rejection rules and sampling bias, are public parameters of the problem. They are not assumed to produce uniform independent ring elements.

The public key is \(P=(\alpha,s)\), where \(s=x+hy\). Define the core encryption map

\[
\mathcal E(P,m;\theta)=\left(r_1+hr_2,\ E(m)+\pi_L(sr_2+e)\right),\qquad (r_1,r_2,e)=S_R(\theta).
\]

The public seed \(\alpha\), not merely its expansion \(h\), is included in the attacker's input. The retained codec is an outer RS\((n_1,16)\) code over \(\mathbb F_{256}\), followed by \(r\)-fold repeated RM\((1,7)\); its field representation, coordinate order and deterministic tie rules are part of \(E,D\).

\(H(P)\) is the concrete, domain-separated SHA3-256 public-key digest. The independent public salt \(z\) is 16 bytes; \(G\)'s first and second 32-byte halves are \(K\) and \(\theta\). A designated random-function response is sampled once for each new input and reused on repeats. Only \(G\) changes between the two experiments; \(H\), the other hash roles and all seed maps remain concrete. All pre-challenge \(G\) calls count toward \(Q\).

This is a bounded comparison of complete-key recovery, not a claim that fixed SHA3 code is indistinguishable from an independent random function for arbitrary tests. It makes no collision-resistance premise about \(H\) in this single-public-key experiment.

Here “best” is a supremum over the declared uniform classical bit-RAM algorithm class, including its work and query limits. The real and ideal suprema may be attained or approached by different algorithms. This is not the stronger claim that each individual program has the same real/ideal success. The model comparison must use compatible conventions for preprocessing, available public information and hash-call accounting.

### Use in this construction

The binding is `hqc@modeled-research-v3`: 66 tuples from `crucible/data/hqc_model_profiles.json`, with \(n_1=16+2\delta\), \(1\le\delta\le15\), and \(1\le r\le3\). The fixed native source is liboqs commit `5a1a854b0dc9f2141bdc771c555ee60c37950183`, with the source/archive and specialization recorded in `docs/hqc-model-v3.txt`. Only the declared parameter headers are specialized. The construction, domain separators and seed maps retain the [2025-08-22 HQC specification](https://pqc-hqc.org/doc/hqc_specifications_2025_08_22.pdf), Sections 3.1–3.6. The 2026 specification is a different construction/parameter target and is not substituted for it.

The local first-target-query argument yields the ideal passive bound \(\min\{1,Q\epsilon_{\rm PKE}(T_B)+2^{-256}\}\). The concrete conclusion must add \(\delta_{\rm hash}(T,Q)\), capped at one. \(T_B\) charges simulation and all other computation; the factor \(Q\) is retained. This model premise is distinct from both correctness premises: it does not say that cyclic-product noise is independent, does not prove decoder correctness, and does not extend the passive argument to full CCA or quantum security.

readable_sections.title: One common measure of attack work
readable_sections.body:
These curves use **Classical bit-RAM v1**: elementary Boolean operations and one-bit memory transfers share a fixed accounting rule. All attack setup is charged to one fresh challenge. Memory capacity is unlimited in this abstraction, and the storage bound remains visible beside the graph.

The plotted quantity is \(\log_2 W\), where \(W\) bounds a specified strategy's work and its stated assumptions imply at least **50% probability of recovering the complete shared key**. These are reproducible **baseline upper bounds**, not the cheapest known attacks or a security lower bound. A bigger value does not establish a more secure scheme. Full text contains the cost rules, proofs, parameter table and reproduction commands.

classic-mceliece@length-research-v1.title: Classic McEliece: unique decoding and an open attack assessment
classic-mceliece@length-research-v1.summary: Fifty shortened Goppa codes keep m=12 and t=64. Distance supports agreement; current attack-cost calibration remains incomplete.

sections.title: The exact Goppa syndrome must hide the error
sections.body:
Encapsulation samples a full weight-64 error \(e\), publishes \(C=He\), and hashes \(e\) with \(C\) to obtain the shared key. In the stated hash model, complete-key recovery implies recovery of that error, apart from a blind 256-bit key guess.

The decoding premise applies to the actual seeded Goppa-key distribution. It includes both direct decoding and recovery of equivalent private structure. No claim that these keys are indistinguishable from arbitrary random codes is needed for this reduction.

sections.title: Scheme security: interpreting structural evidence
sections.body:
The 2026 GIJS work supplies a public-key distinguisher and heuristic extensions to decryption and key recovery. Subsequent work improves recovery costs under explicit success and accounting assumptions. A distinguisher is not automatically shared-key recovery; one modeled run is not automatically a complete success-normalized KEM attack.

Applicable evidence must specify the exact key distribution, algorithm, success model, memory, preprocessing and final decoding/KDF work. The repository's public small-instance verification concerns that instance, not a full-size benchmark. These distinctions explain the ongoing reassessment.

sections.title: A complete passive key-recovery argument
sections.body:
Let \(\epsilon_{\rm SD}(T)\) bound recovery of the exact error at work \(T\). The classical fresh-challenge reduction gives
\[\Pr[\widehat K=K]\le\min\{1,\epsilon_{\rm SD}(T_B)+2^{-256}\}.\]
The reduction checks the adversary’s hash inputs against the public syndrome. The code’s distance makes any valid weight-64 match unique. Full text proves the claim and accounts for these checks.

This says how confidentiality depends on decoding hardness; it supplies no numerical hardness value. It is a passive result, without a decapsulation oracle, rather than a full CCA or quantum-query application.

These inequalities are in the stated oracle model. A concrete-implementation claim must add the separate hash-transfer slack \(\delta_{\rm hash}\) and cap the result at one.

sections.title: Unconditional honest agreement by unique decoding
sections.body:
For any valid binary Goppa key here, the code has minimum distance at least \(2t+1=129\). Thus two errors of weight at most \(t=64\) cannot share a syndrome. The specified bounded-distance decoder returns the unique honest error, and the deterministic session hashes agree. This holds for all fifty supported lengths without a cryptographic hardness or hash-randomness premise.

Full text supplies the distance argument and links it to the decoder’s specification. The claim concerns the mathematical algorithms with valid successful key generation; uniqueness alone does not verify the native executable.

sections.title: Why no current security curve is supplied
sections.body:
The historical Prange proxy is
\[
\log_2\!\left[\binom n{64}/\binom{768}{64}\right].
\]
It counts inverse support-hit probability for a selected 768-coordinate set. Singular-submatrix rejection, elimination, verification, improved decoding and structural attacks are omitted. It is not plotted as calibrated security.

The October 29 study adds source-pinned partial ISD estimates for nine diagnostic tuples under three resource models. Those are offline comparisons, not a new progression or complete best-attack assessment. Their numbers are not silently assigned to the existing fifty stages.

sections.title: Goppa syndrome decoding
sections.body:
Fix \((m,n,t)\) and a declared seeded sampler \(\mathcal S\) for a monic irreducible degree-\(t\) polynomial \(g\) over \(\mathbb F_{2^m}\) and an ordered distinct support \(L\) avoiding its roots. Publish the systematic binary parity-check matrix \(H\) of \(\Gamma(L,g)=\{c\in\mathbb F_2^n:\sum_i c_i/(X-\alpha_i)=0\bmod g\}\), conditioned on successful generation. Independently choose a uniform weight-\(t\) vector \(e\in\mathbb F_2^n\), and publish \(He\). The claim is \(\Pr[A(H,He)=e]\le\epsilon_{\rm SD}(T)\) for every classical algorithm of bit-RAM work at most \(T\). The bound must cover structural attacks on this sampler, not only generic decoding.

Let \(\mathbb F=\mathbb F_{2^m}\). A support \(L=(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n)\) consists of distinct elements of \(\mathbb F\); \(g\in\mathbb F[X]\) is monic and irreducible of degree \(t\), with \(g(\alpha_i)\ne0\). The binary Goppa code is

\[
\Gamma(L,g)=\left\{c\in\mathbb F_2^n:\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{c_i}{X-\alpha_i}=0\pmod{g(X)}\right\}.
\]

The declared sampler \(\mathcal S\) maps a uniformly drawn seed to \((g,L)\) and the systematic-coordinate ordering, retaining its actual retry/success rules. Generate the binary parity-check matrix, perform the specified systematic conversion, and publish \(H=[I_{mt}\mid T]\). Successful generation includes the needed full rank and systematic pivot condition; it does not condition on a later ciphertext or its decapsulation. The actual \(g,L\) remain hidden. This is a distribution over structured Goppa matrices, not uniform binary matrices.

Independently choose \(e\) uniformly from all \(n\)-bit vectors of Hamming weight \(t\), and publish \(c=He\). Winning means returning this exact \(e\). Probability includes the seed, error and attacker's coins; all attacker preprocessing and candidate verification count toward the classical work budget. Binary square-free Goppa distance at least \(2t+1\) ensures that the weight-\(t\) preimage is unique.

### Use in this construction

The binding is `classic-mceliece@length-research-v1`: \(m=12,t=64\), with 50 registered lengths \(840\le n\le3488\). The source-seeded irreducible-Goppa/support generator, systematic ordering, successful-generation behavior and uniform general-parameter fixed-weight error sampler are those retained in `docs/code-research.txt`. The public matrix has 768 rows. The source sampler is part of the claim; it is not silently replaced by uniform sampling of all irreducible polynomials and all supports.

The [Classic McEliece specification](https://classic.mceliece.org/mceliece-spec-20221023.pdf), Sections 4.2–4.4 and 5–6, defines the Goppa, syndrome and hash construction. Its published parameter claims do not automatically apply to the shortened research lengths. The local full argument and the [authors' mathematical decoder](https://classic.mceliece.org/mceliece-sage-20221023/decode.sage.html) justify the algebraic decoder statement; they are not a formal refinement proof of the retained native executable.

No numerical \(\epsilon_{\rm SD}(T)\) is established here. The reduced lengths can be weak, and structural attack evidence must constrain any future bound. Generic random-code decoding hardness or a Prange cost curve is not a substitute. The local passive-key theorem uses this premise at its reduction budget; the separate distance/decoder correctness argument does not depend on computational hardness.

sections.title: Session-key hash transfer
sections.body:
Let \(H\) follow a declared Goppa parity-check distribution and choose an independent uniform weight-\(t\) error \(e\in\mathbb F_2^n\). Set \(c=He\) and \(K=\operatorname{SHAKE256}(1\Vert\operatorname{enc}(e)\Vert\operatorname{enc}(c),32)\). Let \(p_{\rm real}(T,Q)\) be the greatest probability of recovering \(K\) from \((H,c)\) among classical algorithms of work at most \(T\) and \(Q\) designated hash calls. Define \(p_{\rm ideal}\) with only the domain-1 session-key hash replaced by an independent random function to 256 bits. The claim is \(p_{\rm real}(T,Q)\le p_{\rm ideal}(T,Q)+\delta_{\rm hash}(T,Q)\). No small upper bound on the transfer slack is proved.

Let \(\mathbb F=\mathbb F_{2^m}\). A support \(L=(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n)\) consists of distinct elements of \(\mathbb F\); \(g\in\mathbb F[X]\) is monic and irreducible of degree \(t\), with \(g(\alpha_i)\ne0\). The binary Goppa code is

\[
\Gamma(L,g)=\left\{c\in\mathbb F_2^n:\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{c_i}{X-\alpha_i}=0\pmod{g(X)}\right\}.
\]

The declared sampler \(\mathcal S\) maps a uniformly drawn seed to \((g,L)\) and the systematic-coordinate ordering, retaining its actual retry/success rules. Generate the binary parity-check matrix, perform the specified systematic conversion, and publish \(H=[I_{mt}\mid T]\). Successful generation includes the needed full rank and systematic pivot condition; it does not condition on a later ciphertext or its decapsulation. The actual \(g,L\) remain hidden. This is a distribution over structured Goppa matrices, not uniform binary matrices.

Independently choose \(e\) uniformly from all \(n\)-bit vectors of Hamming weight \(t\), and publish \(c=He\). Winning means returning this exact \(e\). Probability includes the seed, error and attacker's coins; all attacker preprocessing and candidate verification count toward the classical work budget. Binary square-free Goppa distance at least \(2t+1\) ensures that the weight-\(t\) preimage is unique.

The leading \(1\) is one byte. \(\operatorname{enc}\) uses the fixed canonical bit packing and lengths of this parameter tuple, so parsing is unambiguous. The random function returns consistent values on repeated inputs and independent uniform 256-bit values on new inputs. Only the session-key role changes between experiments; key-generation expansion remains concrete. All designated calls, including precomputation, count toward \(Q\).

The transfer premise concerns this complete-key-recovery experiment. It is not a claim that the public SHAKE program itself cannot be distinguished from an independent random function. Domain separation makes the modeled roles distinct; it does not prove the transfer.

Here “best” is a supremum over the declared uniform classical bit-RAM algorithm class, including its work and query limits. The real and ideal suprema may be attained or approached by different algorithms. This is not the stronger claim that each individual program has the same real/ideal success. The model comparison must use compatible conventions for preprocessing, available public information and hash-call accounting.

### Use in this construction

The binding is `classic-mceliece@length-research-v1`: \(m=12,t=64\), with 50 registered lengths \(840\le n\le3488\). The source-seeded irreducible-Goppa/support generator, systematic ordering, successful-generation behavior and uniform general-parameter fixed-weight error sampler are those retained in `docs/code-research.txt`. The public matrix has 768 rows. The source sampler is part of the claim; it is not silently replaced by uniform sampling of all irreducible polynomials and all supports.

The [Classic McEliece specification](https://classic.mceliece.org/mceliece-spec-20221023.pdf), Sections 4.2–4.4 and 5–6, defines the Goppa, syndrome and hash construction. Its published parameter claims do not automatically apply to the shortened research lengths. The local full argument and the [authors' mathematical decoder](https://classic.mceliece.org/mceliece-sage-20221023/decode.sage.html) justify the algebraic decoder statement; they are not a formal refinement proof of the retained native executable.

The passive theorem gives ideal success at most \(\min\{1,\epsilon_{\rm SD}(T_B)+2^{-256}\}\), where \(T_B\) includes testing candidate errors from all hash queries. Uniqueness supplies public verification without dividing the success bound by the query count. The concrete conclusion must still add \(\delta_{\rm hash}(T,Q)\), capped at one. No chosen-ciphertext or quantum security conclusion is claimed. Neither this hash premise nor syndrome-decoding hardness is needed for the separate mathematical correctness proof.

sections.title: One common measure of attack work
sections.body:
These curves use **Classical bit-RAM v1**: elementary Boolean operations and one-bit memory transfers share a fixed accounting rule. All attack setup is charged to one fresh challenge. Memory capacity is unlimited in this abstraction, and the storage bound remains visible beside the graph.

The plotted quantity is \(\log_2 W\), where \(W\) bounds a specified strategy's work and its stated assumptions imply at least **50% probability of recovering the complete shared key**. These are reproducible **baseline upper bounds**, not the cheapest known attacks or a security lower bound. A bigger value does not establish a more secure scheme. Full text contains the cost rules, proofs, parameter table and reproduction commands.

sections.title: An information-set decoding attack
sections.body:
Select columns, solve a binary linear system, and check whether the result is the weight-64 ciphertext error. Once recovered, the error and ciphertext give the full shared secret through the specified SHAKE256 derivation. The curve includes all trials and their elimination work. It is a deliberately simple attack budget, not the cheapest known decoding attack or a security lower bound.

For \(r=mt\) parity checks and a weight-\(t\) error, a random \(r\)-column set contains its support with probability \(\pi=\binom rt/\binom nt\). The budget uses \(R=\lceil32/\pi\rceil\) bounded trials, including binary elimination. The rank premise is essential.

sections.title: A-35 · Enough information sets remain invertible
sections.body:
For at least seven eighths of honest targets, at least one eighth of the selected column sets that contain the true error support give an invertible matrix. This is a working hypothesis about the actual structured public matrices; it has not been established for every stage. The curve is conditional on it.

Applies to Stages 1–50.

## Reproducible bit-RAM attack analysis

## Shared computation model: crucible-bit-ram-v1

The program is uniform in public configuration inputs; no answer-dependent
advice is permitted. Its fixed-address bit registers support arbitrary Boolean
functions of one or two bits at unit cost. Constants, fixed wiring and fixed bit
permutations are free. A dynamically addressed bit read or write costs one;
computing that address is additional charged arithmetic. This is a bit-RAM
abstraction inspired by NIST's classical gate-count discussions, not the CAT
pure circuit metric and not a NIST-approved scheme classification.

The baseline has no memory-cap constraint. It measures neither physical latency
nor energy. A pointer of b bits must be manipulated with the b-bit arithmetic
account. Loops use a public counter width and charge increment/comparison.
Input generation for the honest challenger is outside the attack budget; all
attacker initialization, candidate generation, verification and key derivation
are inside. Randomness and any rejection sampling need explicit budgets or
their own success-loss treatment. A counter on high-level Python operations is
validation of the operation census, not a trace of exact elementary gates.

Primitive upper bounds, for width w: ADD/SUB/CMP=8w; MUX=3w;
MODADD=24(w+1); MUL=16(w+1)^2; DIVMOD=64(w+1)^2;
MODMUL=80(w+1)^2; LOOP(b)=16(b+1).
MODPOW(w,e)=e(2 MODMUL(w)+MUX(w)+LOOP(e))+2w.
All bounds refer to schoolbook/ripple, restoring-division and double-and-add
algorithms. They deliberately upper-bound a particular implementation.

SHA-256/SHA-512 follow FIPS180-4. The schedule uses two small sigmas and three
word additions per expanded word. Each round uses two large sigmas, Ch, Maj,
and seven additions. Eight final additions update the chaining value. Padding
and block input/output are charged. SHA3/SHAKE follow FIPS202: Keccak-f[1600]
uses at most193536 Boolean operations (24 rounds of8064), padded to200000
for control. Absorption and output transfers are additional. These are
algorithmic upper bounds, not claims about optimized hardware.

Every profile's complete attack is stopped within its reported budget. Its
success statement names the probability space and any unproved premises.
The resulting curve is a documented attack upper bound, not a proven security
level and not necessarily the cheapest known attack. No 50%-success result is
inferred simply by dividing cost by average success probability.

Primary specifications:
- https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/FIPS/NIST.FIPS.180-4.pdf
- https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/FIPS/NIST.FIPS.202.pdf


## Reproduction

From this source checkout:
```text
python scripts/build_ram_attack_notes.py --check
python -m pytest tests/test_ram_common.py tests/test_ram_classical_attacks.py tests/test_ram_lattice_attacks.py tests/test_ram_code_attacks.py tests/test_ram_catalogue.py
```
The generated `crucible/data/ram_attack_curves.json` retains integer cost components, parameters, assumptions and source-file hashes. No cryptographic-size attack is executed. Small examples check implementation paths; they do not verify heuristic premises at large sizes. No external model service or paid API is used.

## An information-set decoding attack

Worked configuration: classic-mceliece-length-research-v1-tier-50. The same algorithm and parameterized formulas generate the other rows below.

## Attack specification: explicit Prange baseline

For the actual binary Goppa public matrix H=[I_(mt)|T], N=n, r=mt=768,
t=64. The ciphertext is s=He. Select an r-column set J uniformly, solve
H_J z=s, extend z by zeros, and accept only a weight-t vector with syndrome s.
The code distance is at least2t+1, so two accepted weight-t vectors cannot
differ: their difference would be a nonzero codeword of weight<=2t. Thus an
accepted vector is the honest error. Derive the full secret by
SHAKE256(0x01 || little_endian_bits(e) || ciphertext,32).

For any fixed support, hit=binom(r,t)/binom(N,t). Rank is NOT independent of
the support hit and is NOT inferred from a uniform-matrix constant. The visible
rank-density hypothesis supplies rho>=1/8 on a target set of measure>=7/8.
Bounded partial Fisher-Yates uses up to64 rejection draws per index, each with
ceil(log2(N-i)) random bits when N-i elements remain. Thus each draw is accepted
with probability>=1/2. Its abort probability is <=r*2^-64<1/2.
Conditioned on not aborting, the resulting r-subset remains uniform. Therefore
each independent trial on a good target succeeds with probability>=hit/16.
R=ceil(32/hit) gives failure<exp(-2)<1/4. Overall success is >=21/32>1/2.

The bit-RAM budget includes the index-array initialization and bounded sampler,
matrix extraction, pivot search, row swaps/XOR elimination, support weight and
syndrome verification, and the KDF. Addresses use the declared bit width.
Store contiguous rows and maintain their base pointers by additions; do not
recompute row*stride with an uncharged integer multiply on every access. The
memory account includes the row-base pointer arrays. Extraction has r(r+1)
cell slots; elimination is bounded by
r^3+4r^2+4r slots; verification uses rN+4N slots. Each slot pays
8+4 LOOP(a)+4 ADD(a), covering bit transfers, Boolean work, address changes
and nested-loop control. A separate R.bit_length()-wide trial counter is charged
per trial, rather than truncating that counter to an address width. No
high-level Gaussian elimination is counted as one
operation. The matrix and scratch storage are also reported. Exact integer
budgets are preserved before taking logarithms.

This is a conservative upper bound for the specified Prange implementation.
It excludes faster ISD, structural Goppa attacks and quantum attacks; it cannot
be used as a lower bound on security. The tests exhaust tiny information sets,
verify the exact hit/rank product, and execute recovery; they do not validate
the structured-rank hypothesis for the current cryptographic profiles.


Success statement for this worked configuration: 21/32 > 1/2, conditional on the stated rank-density hypothesis

## A-35 · Enough information sets remain invertible

Write H as an r-by-N binary matrix and e for the actual weight-t target. With probability at least7/8 over the honest target draw, Pr_J[rank(H_J)=r | supp(e) subset J] >=1/8, where J is uniform among r-subsets. This is a per-instance density condition on a 7/8-measure good set, not an average success probability that can be amplified without justification. Fresh trials are independent conditional on H,e. Neither random-matrix heuristics nor toy checks prove this claim for binary Goppa or quasi-cyclic matrices.

classic-mceliece@length-research-v1.full_text_argument_appendix:
## Exact security and correctness argument: Classic McEliece length research v1

### Distribution, game and conditional theorem

Fix an exact registered length n (840 through 3488), field degree m=12 and Goppa degree t=64. Generate the seeded irreducible-Goppa/support key using the pinned research process; condition on successful systematic key generation, not on passing a later agreement test. The public parity-check matrix is H=[I_768|T]. Draw e uniformly among the weight-64 n-bit vectors by the specified general-parameter FixedWeight algorithm. Publish C=He. The honest key is SHAKE256(byte(1)||LEbits(e)||C,32).

Define OW_SD(T) as the best classical success probability at work T of recovering e from (H,C) under exactly that distribution. This incorporates arbitrary use of Goppa structure, not just generic information-set decoding. No assertion is made that the selected parameters have a particular value of OW_SD(T). The plotted Prange curve is an upper bound for an attack and cannot establish a small value of this success function.

Replace only the domain-1 session hash by an independent random oracle to 256 bits, with other public expansion roles treated separately. For an adversary A receiving (H,C) and returning the full key, construct B with the same input. B lazily answers A's hash queries. For every query of the exact form byte(1)||e'||C, check length/canonical encoding, wt(e')=64, and He'=C. If the checks pass, output e'. The distance proof below makes this the actual honest error. This uses no secret key, no stored target and no correctness oracle.

If A queries the target hash input, B succeeds. If it never does, the actual target key is an unqueried independent uniform 256-bit string; A's single final output equals it with probability at most 2^-256. Thus

    Pr[A recovers K] <= min(1, OW_SD(T_B) + 2^-256).

T_B includes A, oracle simulation, parsing/weight checks and at most q_H public matrix-vector products for q_H relevant queries. The theorem has no hidden factoring/random-code or code-indistinguishability premise. It has two visible dependencies: exact-distribution decoding hardness at a specified budget, and the oracle model for the session hash. A fixed SHAKE implementation is not proved equivalent to that model.

The same query-hiding argument gives a passive key-indistinguishability statement under a chosen convention for distinguishing advantage; the displayed theorem intentionally uses the site's concrete whole-key recovery event. This is not a complete CCA, quantum-query, multi-target or side-channel argument. Published stronger transforms have their own hypotheses and loss accounting. This elementary passive reduction is authored here and manually checked.

### Why the honest target is unique

Let L=(alpha_i) be distinct field elements and let g be the monic irreducible Goppa polynomial of degree t, with no support root. For a nonzero binary Goppa codeword c with support S, set f(X)=product_{i in S}(X-alpha_i). The Goppa relation says g divides f'(X)/f(X) modulo g. Since gcd(f,g)=1, g divides f'. In characteristic two, every exponent in f' is even, so f' is a square polynomial over the finite field. As g is square-free, g^2 divides f'. But f is a product of distinct factors, so f' is nonzero. Therefore deg(f')>=2t, while deg(f')<=|S|-1. Hence |S|>=2t+1.

If e,e' both have weight at most t and He=He', their difference is a codeword of weight at most 2t. The distance result forces e=e'. Shortening to any registered subset L of n distinct support points preserves this proof; it does not require n to remain at the published endpoint.

The specified Decode algorithm in the 2022 specification, Section 4.4, first embeds C into v=(C,0,...,0). Since H=[I|T], Hv=C. For an honest e, c=v+e satisfies Hc=0 and d(c,v)=wt(e)=t. The Decode algorithm is the specified bounded-distance operation of the 2022 specification, Section 4.4, with its Goppa decoding subroutine (the authors' Sage reference is decode.sage/goppa.sage); by this algorithm contract it returns this unique c, and hence e=v+c; its weight and syndrome checks pass. Both parties then hash the same bytes. Honest agreement is therefore exact for the mathematical algorithms. SHAKE can even have collisions without changing this equality.

This theorem does not prove an arbitrary program realizes the specified decoder. The retained PQClean native decoder and research parameter specialization are separately checked through native agreement, reviewed patches and endpoint vectors where their source/KAT fixtures are available. No new native functional-correctness proof is asserted.

### Reproduction and sources

Construction, decoding and hash framing: Classic McEliece specification 2022-10-23, Sections 4.3–4.4, 5.4–5.6 and 6. The elementary logarithmic-derivative distance argument above is written out here. The security guide's Section 5 distinguishes generic CCA-transform results from the underlying one-way decoding premise.

Current code-length and FixedWeight batch formulas are in crucible/code_parameters.py; actual wrapper/patch scope is in crucible/code_native.py and scripts/code_build_backend.py. `python -m pytest -q tests/test_code_research.py -k every_research_profile` exercises native honest agreement for the retained code workers. `tests/test_code_research.py` also has sampler-source and endpoint KAT checks; those require the original extracted build/KAT fixtures, not only installed executables. None of these tests verifies the computational-hardness or oracle premise.

### Transfer to concrete hashing

The inequalities above are mathematical claims in the specified ideal experiment. For the concrete hash roles, the separate premise bounds the concrete key-recovery probability by that ideal probability plus delta_hash(T,Q), for the explicitly declared algorithm and resource class. Add this term to the right side and cap at one. No small numerical value of delta_hash is proved here. This is an operational, construction-specific transfer premise; it does not assert that an adversary cannot distinguish a publicly computable fixed SHA function from a freshly sampled oracle by directly comparing their outputs. A generic collision-resistance statement would not justify the transfer.

statements.label: A-25
statements.title: Goppa syndrome decoding
statements.definition: Fix \((m,n,t)\) and a declared seeded sampler \(\mathcal S\) for a monic irreducible degree-\(t\) polynomial \(g\) over \(\mathbb F_{2^m}\) and an ordered distinct support \(L\) avoiding its roots. Publish the systematic binary parity-check matrix \(H\) of \(\Gamma(L,g)=\{c\in\mathbb F_2^n:\sum_i c_i/(X-\alpha_i)=0\bmod g\}\), conditioned on successful generation. Independently choose a uniform weight-\(t\) vector \(e\in\mathbb F_2^n\), and publish \(He\). The claim is \(\Pr[A(H,He)=e]\le\epsilon_{\rm SD}(T)\) for every classical algorithm of bit-RAM work at most \(T\). The bound must cover structural attacks on this sampler, not only generic decoding.

statements.label: A-26
statements.title: Session-key hash transfer
statements.definition: Let \(H\) follow a declared Goppa parity-check distribution and choose an independent uniform weight-\(t\) error \(e\in\mathbb F_2^n\). Set \(c=He\) and \(K=\operatorname{SHAKE256}(1\Vert\operatorname{enc}(e)\Vert\operatorname{enc}(c),32)\). Let \(p_{\rm real}(T,Q)\) be the greatest probability of recovering \(K\) from \((H,c)\) among classical algorithms of work at most \(T\) and \(Q\) designated hash calls. Define \(p_{\rm ideal}\) with only the domain-1 session-key hash replaced by an independent random function to 256 bits. The claim is \(p_{\rm real}(T,Q)\le p_{\rm ideal}(T,Q)+\delta_{\rm hash}(T,Q)\). No small upper bound on the transfer slack is proved.

statements.label: Security claim
statements.title: Passive shared-key recovery bound
statements.definition:
For every registered native configuration of exact research release `classic-mceliece@length-research-v1`, generate one fresh honest public key and one encapsulation. Let R be the supremum probability, among classical adversaries using at most T total computation work and the stated query budgets, of returning the complete 256-bit shared key in one output. Probability includes honest generation, encapsulation and the adversary's coins; condition on valid successful generation. Pre-challenge computation and designated hash queries count toward the same budgets.

\[R\le\min\{1,\epsilon_{\rm SD}(T_B)+2^{-256}+\delta_{\rm hash}(T,Q)\}.\]

\(\epsilon_{\rm SD}(T_B)\) bounds the greatest success, at work \(T_B\), of recovering the uniform weight-64 honest error \(e\) from \((H,He)\) for the exact seeded binary-Goppa/support distribution at the registered length, conditioned on successful systematic key generation. This success function includes structural attacks. \(Q\) bounds designated session-hash queries, and \(T_B\) includes the adversary, oracle simulation, canonical parsing, weight checks and at most \(Q\) public matrix-vector products. \(\delta_{\rm hash}(T,Q)\) bounds excess recovery when the concrete domain-1 SHAKE session hash replaces an independent random function to 256 bits; all other expansion roles remain fixed.

No decapsulation, key-checking or leakage oracle is available. The bounds concern a single classical target; they do not assert CCA, quantum or multi-target security. The success/advantage bounds and hash-transfer slack are explicit parameters, not numerically certified small values.

statements.label: Correctness claim
statements.title: Honest key agreement
statements.definition:
For every registered native configuration of exact research release `classic-mceliece@length-research-v1`, run honest \((pk,sk)\leftarrow\mathsf{KeyGen}\), \((C,K)\leftarrow\mathsf{Encaps}(pk)\) and \(K'=\mathsf{Decaps}(sk,C)\) using its specified samplers, mathematical algorithms, exact arithmetic and canonical encodings. Condition on valid successful key generation and completed operations, never on agreement.

The claim is \(\Pr[K'\ne K]\le d\), averaged over the honest keys and encapsulation randomness, with \(d=0\) for every allowed weight-64 honest error at each registered length.

These are mathematical statements about the specified algorithms. They exclude invalid inputs, entropy or implementation faults, runtime aborts and side channels; they do not certify native executable correctness.

readable_sections.title: The exact Goppa syndrome must hide the error
readable_sections.body:
Encapsulation samples a full weight-64 error \(e\), publishes \(C=He\), and hashes \(e\) with \(C\) to obtain the shared key. In the stated hash model, complete-key recovery implies recovery of that error, apart from a blind 256-bit key guess.

The decoding premise applies to the actual seeded Goppa-key distribution. It includes both direct decoding and recovery of equivalent private structure. No claim that these keys are indistinguishable from arbitrary random codes is needed for this reduction.

readable_sections.title: Scheme security: interpreting structural evidence
readable_sections.body:
The 2026 GIJS work supplies a public-key distinguisher and heuristic extensions to decryption and key recovery. Subsequent work improves recovery costs under explicit success and accounting assumptions. A distinguisher is not automatically shared-key recovery; one modeled run is not automatically a complete success-normalized KEM attack.

Applicable evidence must specify the exact key distribution, algorithm, success model, memory, preprocessing and final decoding/KDF work. The repository's public small-instance verification concerns that instance, not a full-size benchmark. These distinctions explain the ongoing reassessment.

readable_sections.title: A complete passive key-recovery argument
readable_sections.body:
Let \(\epsilon_{\rm SD}(T)\) bound recovery of the exact error at work \(T\). The classical fresh-challenge reduction gives
\[\Pr[\widehat K=K]\le\min\{1,\epsilon_{\rm SD}(T_B)+2^{-256}\}.\]
The reduction checks the adversary’s hash inputs against the public syndrome. The code’s distance makes any valid weight-64 match unique. Full text proves the claim and accounts for these checks.

This says how confidentiality depends on decoding hardness; it supplies no numerical hardness value. It is a passive result, without a decapsulation oracle, rather than a full CCA or quantum-query application.

These inequalities are in the stated oracle model. A concrete-implementation claim must add the separate hash-transfer slack \(\delta_{\rm hash}\) and cap the result at one.

readable_sections.title: Unconditional honest agreement by unique decoding
readable_sections.body:
For any valid binary Goppa key here, the code has minimum distance at least \(2t+1=129\). Thus two errors of weight at most \(t=64\) cannot share a syndrome. The specified bounded-distance decoder returns the unique honest error, and the deterministic session hashes agree. This holds for all fifty supported lengths without a cryptographic hardness or hash-randomness premise.

Full text supplies the distance argument and links it to the decoder’s specification. The claim concerns the mathematical algorithms with valid successful key generation; uniqueness alone does not verify the native executable.

readable_sections.title: Goppa syndrome decoding
readable_sections.body:
Let \(\mathbb F=\mathbb F_{2^m}\). A support \(L=(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n)\) consists of distinct elements of \(\mathbb F\); \(g\in\mathbb F[X]\) is monic and irreducible of degree \(t\), with \(g(\alpha_i)\ne0\). The binary Goppa code is

\[
\Gamma(L,g)=\left\{c\in\mathbb F_2^n:\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{c_i}{X-\alpha_i}=0\pmod{g(X)}\right\}.
\]

The declared sampler \(\mathcal S\) maps a uniformly drawn seed to \((g,L)\) and the systematic-coordinate ordering, retaining its actual retry/success rules. Generate the binary parity-check matrix, perform the specified systematic conversion, and publish \(H=[I_{mt}\mid T]\). Successful generation includes the needed full rank and systematic pivot condition; it does not condition on a later ciphertext or its decapsulation. The actual \(g,L\) remain hidden. This is a distribution over structured Goppa matrices, not uniform binary matrices.

Independently choose \(e\) uniformly from all \(n\)-bit vectors of Hamming weight \(t\), and publish \(c=He\). Winning means returning this exact \(e\). Probability includes the seed, error and attacker's coins; all attacker preprocessing and candidate verification count toward the classical work budget. Binary square-free Goppa distance at least \(2t+1\) ensures that the weight-\(t\) preimage is unique.

### Use in this construction

The binding is `classic-mceliece@length-research-v1`: \(m=12,t=64\), with 50 registered lengths \(840\le n\le3488\). The source-seeded irreducible-Goppa/support generator, systematic ordering, successful-generation behavior and uniform general-parameter fixed-weight error sampler are those retained in `docs/code-research.txt`. The public matrix has 768 rows. The source sampler is part of the claim; it is not silently replaced by uniform sampling of all irreducible polynomials and all supports.

The [Classic McEliece specification](https://classic.mceliece.org/mceliece-spec-20221023.pdf), Sections 4.2–4.4 and 5–6, defines the Goppa, syndrome and hash construction. Its published parameter claims do not automatically apply to the shortened research lengths. The local full argument and the [authors' mathematical decoder](https://classic.mceliece.org/mceliece-sage-20221023/decode.sage.html) justify the algebraic decoder statement; they are not a formal refinement proof of the retained native executable.

No numerical \(\epsilon_{\rm SD}(T)\) is established here. The reduced lengths can be weak, and structural attack evidence must constrain any future bound. Generic random-code decoding hardness or a Prange cost curve is not a substitute. The local passive-key theorem uses this premise at its reduction budget; the separate distance/decoder correctness argument does not depend on computational hardness.

The transfer premise concerns this complete-key-recovery experiment. It is not a claim that the public SHAKE program itself cannot be distinguished from an independent random function. Domain separation makes the modeled roles distinct; it does not prove the transfer.

Here “best” is a supremum over the declared uniform classical bit-RAM algorithm class, including its work and query limits. The real and ideal suprema may be attained or approached by different algorithms. This is not the stronger claim that each individual program has the same real/ideal success. readable_sections.title: One common measure of attack work
readable_sections.body:
These curves use **Classical bit-RAM v1**: elementary Boolean operations and one-bit memory transfers share a fixed accounting rule. All attack setup is charged to one fresh challenge. Memory capacity is unlimited in this abstraction, and the storage bound remains visible beside the graph.

The plotted quantity is \(\log_2 W\), where \(W\) bounds a specified strategy's work and its stated assumptions imply at least **50% probability of recovering the complete shared key**. These are reproducible **baseline upper bounds**, not the cheapest known attacks or a security lower bound. A bigger value does not establish a more secure scheme. Full text contains the cost rules, proofs, parameter table and reproduction commands.

readable_sections.title: An information-set decoding attack
readable_sections.body:
Select columns, solve a binary linear system, and check whether the result is the weight-64 ciphertext error. Once recovered, the error and ciphertext give the full shared secret through the specified SHAKE256 derivation. The curve includes all trials and their elimination work. It is a deliberately simple attack budget, not the cheapest known decoding attack or a security lower bound.

For \(r=mt\) parity checks and a weight-\(t\) error, a random \(r\)-column set contains its support with probability \(\pi=\binom rt/\binom nt\). The budget uses \(R=\lceil32/\pi\rceil\) bounded trials, including binary elimination. The rank premise is essential.
